column20: The disproportionate impact of climate change is rooted in the growth of the city and the social construct. Austin has a long history of systemic racism and racial inequity that continues to impact communities in the Eastern Crescent. Throughout Austin's history, communities of color have been excluded, marginalized, and discriminated against as a result of City policies and practices. This has led to a disproportionate impact of air pollution, heat exposure and flood risk in historically Black and Latinx neighborhoods due to industrialization and inadequate infrastructure. Working with faculty at the University of Texas at Austin, students and staff conducted a multi-risk assessment that considers how social vulnerability and hazard risk interact. The findings identify specific neighbourhoods (spatially designated as census block groups) that score relatively high on social vulnerability and face relatively high hazard risk.The health-related multi-risk assessment considers hazard and vulnerability interactions. In some socially vulnerable census block groups, there may exist risk from a single hazard. In other census block groups, the exposure to multiple hazard risks is relatively high. The possibility of cascading or domino effects amplify the overall risk and present challenges to community resilience. The spatial exposure of independent hazards include: a. Flooding (specifically, riverine/creek flooding) b. Wildfire & grassfires c. Extreme heat d. Drought/Air Quality and, e. unexpected hazards such as severe cold. These hazards can lead to or perpetuate a multitude of health conditions, including respiratory and cardiovascular diseases.

column20: Climate change affects health and quality of life but it doesn't affect everyone in the same way. Climate justice has to do with inequalities: factors such as physical condition, health, age, gender, socio-economic situation or the conditions in the environments we live and work in determine the extent to which climate change affects people. In fact, it is believed that the climate crisis is thebiggest threat to health this century. Sustained, excessive heat leads to an increase in mortality and morbidity, especially among the most vulnerable groups of human beings, but also the rest of the natural world. It is estimated that in 2024, heat was responsible for 50 deaths among men and 185 among women in Barcelona, mostly among older people. To reduce the vulnerability of people to climate change, we need to work on ensuring the continuity of services and universal access to basic supplies, guaranteeing thermal comfort both inside buildings (housing, facilities, etc.) and in public spaces, as well as improving and adapting the services to dependent persons. We need to advance towards becoming a healthy city that ensures the health and well-being of its citizens. A socially just city that reduces inequalities. And a habitable, comfortable city with quality public spaces. Most important challenges in Barcelona are:• Reducing the vulnerability of people to the climate crisis, understood to mean those situations that mean some people adapt less well to their effects, either because of their socio-economic situation (family income, housing conditions, doing demandingphysical activities outdoors), characteristics (gender, age, situation of solitude) or health (people with limited autonomy, chronic diseases, etc).• Cutting NOx and PM emissions, the main local pollutants which directly affect the health of Barcelona's population and that of the surrounding area.• Reducing vulnerability and energy poverty.• Improving thermal and acoustic comfort in the city: in homes, sensitive facilities and public spaces.• Improving our knowledge of the impact climate change has on health, as well as social and gender inequalities.• Preventing and controlling possible alterations in the geographical and seasonal distribution of vectors (mosquitoes and others) and the diseases they can transmit.•Improving the accessibility (physical and economic) of healthy, fair-trade and sustainable foods, especially among people in a vulnerable situation.• Promoting healthier diets low in emissions: more local, fresh and seasonal produce, more fruit and vegetables, more ecological produce, less packaging, fewer highly processed foods, reducing the consumption of animal protein (above all red meat) and prioritising meat that comes from extensive and ecological stockbreeding

column20: There are concentrated poor neighbourhoods of ingrained poverty, poor housing, health and environment that are getting worse with time not better. The city is less resilient to external impacts, climate or Covid-19. More development in the city will lead to more localised flooding if adequate surfaces are not provided. Climate change will lead to extreme weathers and cause disruption and damage to the infrastructure and services and more tropical diseases will put strain on the local health services and facilities. As previously outlined extreme heat has the risk to exacerbate illness in the most vulnerable. In 2022 (most recent available as of Jul 25), 24% of the 443,703 households across Birmingham are classed as being in fuel poverty - the second highest in the whole country (where the average was 13.1%). Sub regional fuel poverty data published by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in December 2024 (2022 data) shows the Parliamentary Constituency area of Hodge Hill was the most fuel poor, at an incidence of 32.1%. University hospitals Birmingham have conducted a study into the impacts of climate change on the delivery of health services in the city. The study found the following likely impacts: More pregnancy complications, including low birth weight, stillbirth and neonatal admissions, particularly linked to periods of extreme heat. More respiratory illness, renal disease and heat exposure, which is likely to have the most significant impacts on younger children we care for. New patterns of vector-borne illnesses, such as Lyme disease and tick-borne encephalitis have already been seen, and new patterns of malaria and west nile virus will affect travellers to a much wider range of countries. Mental health conditions linked to the impact of extreme weather events (e.g. flooding), as well as anxiety about the changing climate, and the mental health effects of increased economic hardship linked to the costs of our climate deteriorating. Health inequalities (avoidable differences in health outcomes) are likely to widen as those already affected by social deprivation are most likely to be impacted by climate change.

column20: In 2019, in Greater London, the equivalent of between 3,600 to 4,100 premature deaths were estimated to be attributable to air pollution, considering that health effects exist even at very low levels. Some hospitals and other health settings are not currently adapted for the heat and the workforce and patients are at risk, and health service provision could be impacted. There is good evidence that cognitive function is impaired at high temperatures frontline healthcare workers have reported struggling to deliver services in hot weather. There have been reported incidents of hot weather affecting the IT infrastructure of healthcare settings. 
Increased demand for services: Heatwaves lead to a surge in admissions for heat-related illnesses like heatstroke and dehydration, as well as exacerbations of existing conditions such as cardiovascular and respiratory illnesses. Emergency departments are particularly impacted, experiencing overcrowding, increased pressure on staff and finances.
Infrastructure limitations: Many hospitals and other healthcare facilities are not adequately equipped to handle extreme temperatures, especially older buildings lacking effective cooling systems like air conditioning. According to The BMJ, almost half of NHS trusts in England reported at least one overheating incident in wards or clinical areas in 2020-21. There is a lack of funding for adaptation retrofit of existing infrastructure. 
Staff welfare and performance: High temperatures can lead to staff fatigue, decreased cognitive function, and burnout, impacting patient care and potentially exacerbating staff shortages. 
Medication and equipment sensitivity: Some medications require specific temperature storage, and heatwaves can pose risks to their efficacy and availability if storage conditions are compromised. Extreme heat can also impact the function of medical equipment such as MRI scanners and air conditioning units.

Essex County Council (ECC) has been mapping climate change impacts on health and wellbeing with emphasis on groups who are most exposed to effects of extreme weather, flooding, drought, soil degradation, loss of green space/green cover, erosion, water stress and heatwave events. We know that some vulnerable groups face particular health risks from climate change, including the young, the elderly, people with pre-existing health conditions and disabilities and those on low incomes. We are also acutely aware of the positive impact of nature and green spaces on physical and mental health and social wellbeing. The impact of climate change on health outcomes was a cross-cutting theme highlighted in the report 'Net Zero: Making Essex Carbon Neutral', produced by the Essex Climate Action Commission (ECAC), (https://www.essexclimate.org.uk/sites/default/files/DS21_7178%20ECAC_Commission_Report-Final.pdf ) 

ECC works with partners from across the Health Sector to better understand, document and amplify the health benefits of climate action, for example through the Essex Climate Action Commission and the Essex Air Quality Working Group which brings together NHS and local authority officers to look at system-wide actions to improve air quality across Essex.
ECC's Climate Action Plan, developed in response to the ECAC report and recommendations, includes a range of climate-related projects that contribute directly and indirectly to the strategic aim 'Health, wellbeing & independence for all ages' including: •Sustainable Drainage (SuDS) in Schools: Sustainable drainage systems delivered to eight selected Essex schools in Basildon, identified as at high flood risk. 
•Essex Forest Initiative: Part of a five year project to plant 375,000 trees across Essex. 
•Warm Homes Essex Advice Service: advice service delivered by Citizens Advice Essex that provides bespoke support for residents whose health is impacted by living in a cold home. 
•The Jaywick and District Energy Hub is supporting residents with their energy and helping them save money on their energy bills. Residents can get help with free home energy visits, home energy grant applications and more. 
•Local Energy - Innovate UK Pathfinder Places 2 - SHIFT To Net Zero Communities: Innovate UK grant funding to accelerate investment in net zero projects in schools, support for SMEs, and decarbonising heat.•Essex Design Guide Development & Support: Working with the Essex Planning Officers Association (EPOA) to support development of best practise guidance to inform local plan development across Essex. 
•Retrofit Grants for Fuel Poor Houses: Green Homes Grant Local Authority Delivery Phase 2, Sustainable Warmth, Home Upgrade Grant (HUG) 2•Essex Housing: Net zero housing pilot of ten homes, net zero in construction and in use. 
•Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund (SHDF) Wave 1: Grant funded programme to retrofit social housing stock, working with registered housing providers Sanctuary Housing and Eastlight Community Homes. 
•Safer, Greener, Healthier Essex: Using targeted online advertising, social media, PR, and events, as well as collaborating with key partners to encourage modal shift. 
•Bus Services Improvement Plan (BSIP): Rebuild the Essex bus network, reverse the long-term decline in passengers, deliver modal shift from cars and improve public health

column20: Air pollution and climate change are closely related. As well as driving climate change, the main cause of CO2 emissions - the extraction and burning of fossil fuels - is also a major source of air pollutants. What's more, many air pollutants contribute to climate change by affecting the amount of incoming sunlight that is reflected or absorbed by the atmosphere, with some pollutants warming and others cooling the Earth. These short-lived climate-forcing pollutants (SLCPs) include methane, black carbon, ground-level ozone, and sulphate aerosols. They have significant impacts on the climate: black carbon and methane in particular are among the top contributors to global warming after CO2.Poor air quality is the largest environmental risk to the public's health. Taking action to improve air quality is crucial to improve the health of the general population. Whilst air quality has been generally improving over time, particular pollutants remain a serious concern in many urban areas including across Manchester.Air pollution affects the health of people living, working and travelling in Greater Manchester. Pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide (NO2) which is the harmful oxide of nitrogen (NOx), and particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) that are not visible to the naked eye are found at dangerous levels in many urban areas and on busy roads. Road transport causes two-thirds of NOx emissions and nearly 80% of PM emissions at the roadside. Diesel vehicles are the main source of road-based NOx emissions in Greater Manchester, and older vehicles are typically more polluting than newer vehicles. Large vehicles such as lorries are the most polluting from the exhaust pipe, and in general, diesel vehicles contribute the most. Breathing in polluted air contributes to the equivalent of 1,200 deaths a year in Greater Manchester. Both long and short term exposure to air pollution are known to adversely affect health. It affects people's lungs in the short and long term, worsening respiratory issues such as asthma or bronchitis, as well as cardiovascular problems, and reduces life expectancy. Health damage caused by air pollution can begin as early as a baby's first few weeks in the womb and exposure over a long time can lead to heart and lung disease. The most vulnerable in society are hit hardest - children, older people and those already in poor health. Everyone is at risk. But people who spend more time in areas with a high concentration of air pollution are most affected - which can include drivers. The air you breathe inside your vehicle can be dirtier than the air outside so people who spend a lot of time in their cars, taxis, vans or lorries are particularly at risk. The people living in places with the dirtiest air are often those least likely to drive, and some of the Greater Manchester's most deprived communities suffer the worst air pollution as they live close to busy roads. In total, it is estimated that the health and social care costs of air pollution in England could reach £5.3 billion by 2035 unless action is taken. Changing the vehicles we drive and how we travel can clean up our air. This will require residents and businesses to take action, with Greater Manchester's local authorities leading the way. Action is already underway, and this Clean Air Plan will bring forward Measures to bring illegally high roadside NO2 levels within legal limits as soon as possible.

column20: Further work is needed on this topic. This will be undertaken by the 'Manchester Health, Wellbeing and Climate Change Independent Advisory Group, established Q1 2022. This has been scoped in Manchester Climate Risk: a framework for understanding hazards and vulnerability. This report, published in May 2021 states: The adverse direct impacts of climate change - particularly from flooding and higher summer temperatures/ heatwaves - on human health could be considerable. They will involve both exacerbating existing health inequalities and the introduction of new health risks for people. Notably, Greater Manchester is referred to as a 'Marmot city-region'; a place necessitating innovative cross sectoral governance responses to address significant health in-equalities (Codling & Allen, 2020). Health inequalities and the impacts on recovery from shocks were further demonstrated by recent work by Public Health England (2020) outlining disparities in the risk and outcomes from COVID19 across a range of population characteristics (see also Marmot et al, 2020).The human health impacts of climate change may disproportionately affect those who are already vulnerable, for example, older people, very young people, people living in socio-economic deprivation and those with underlying health conditions. Demonstrating this, heatwaves and air pollution exacerbated by climate conditions or moorland fires can cause death and serious illness, particularly in the elderly, children and those with pre-existing respiratory illness and cardio-vascular disease. Flood water poses a (relatively small) risk of drowning and may harbour disease. Households that flood, but for whatever reason are unable to relocate either during the flood event or the process of reconstruction, report ill-health from living in damp homes. Experience of hazards can generate severe mental health and emotional impacts that may outlast the immediate impacts of events. For instance, communities that have suffered from flooding often report impacts in mental health several years after specific flood events. In the longer-term, climate change could increase the risk of new pathogens and diseases borne by invasive insect species. It is possible that warmer summers and milder winters will encourage greater use of the outdoors and greenspace, potentially bringing benefits to physical and mental health.

There are two key dimensions to this: 1.How climate change will directly impact staff, facilities and the effective delivery of essential human health and social care services. For instance, heatwaves may put pressure on acute medical services. Dislocation from floods and storms might increase pressure on social services and GP services. There may also be longer term stresses on services given that climate change is likely to increase chronic physical and mental health challenges.

column20: Increasing temperatures are expected to become a challenge for Newcastle as a result of climate change. We will use the Heatwave Plan for England to prepare for, alert people to, and prevent, the major avoidable effects on health during periods of severe heat in England. Newcastle City Council's Public Health team in partnership with city partners (such as the hospital trust, the physical and mental health trusts, etc) is planning to produce a Heatwave Plan for the city to localise the risks and actions set out in Heatwave Plan for England, and to prepare the city's residents and infrastructure for the increasing severity and frequency of heatwaves due to climate change. We have worked with the Met Office to prepare a Heat Pack which comprises the following:- A summary of why cities are particularly vulnerable to heat.- A description of what the impacts of extreme heat are.- An analysis of how temperature is changing across the UK in relation to current trends and projected future trends in various climate change scenarios including average summer temperatures and hot spell impacts.- An analysis of how temperature is likely to change in Newcastle in a forward projection to the period 2060 - 2080 based on observed temperature trends to date and various climate change scenarios.- Analysis of expected extreme heat events including heatwave frequency, heatwave length, heatwave peak temperature, number of days per year > 30degC / 25degC / 22degC and number of nights per year > 15degC.- Examples of impacts at different temperature thresholds including impacts on water consumption, energy demand for cooling, health and discomfort impacts, heat related illness and mortality particularly among vulnerable populations, increased risk of heat-related health conditions and mortality, infrastructure impacts such as buckling rail tracks, overhead power lines becoming less efficient, etc.- Assessment of how heat impacts vary spatially across a city.- Heatwave planning, co-ordination and response including early warning systems, planning preparation and action to address heatwaves.- Targeted advice to residents during a heatwave- Analysis of how to build longer term urban heat resilience. Climate change related hazards have already affected Northumberland and will continue to increase in frequency and intensity in the future. It is still not fully understood how climate hazards will compound and cascade, either with/from other climate hazards and/or with additional regional/national/international risks. NCC are aware of the Climate change Hazards and Risks for the UK as outlined in the UK Climate Change Risk Assessment 2022 and other supporting reports like the climate change committee's independent assessments, and those of the IPCC. This information has also been supplemented via the met office 'Local Authority

Climate Service' and their local authority climate risk report. There are links between expected climate change hazards, and those found in the Community Risk Register for Northumbria. As such NCC is already well equipped to support communities (as part of the civil contingencies response) when faced some of these risks, e.g. flooding and adverse weather. Alongside this there is also the role NCC plays in protecting and enhancing Northumberland's environment, in particular the greenspaces that are open and free-for-use by Northumberland's communities - these spaces are both a mitigation and adaptation to climate change, while simultaneously supporting the health and wellbeing of communities. Alongside possible Hazards, it is possible to gain understanding the potential vulnerabilities (e.g. age, deprivation/inequalities etc) of Northumberland's population, as a means to help understand climate change risk and adaptation needs, and priorities in the county. NCC is currently collaborating with the Institute of Health Equity to better understand and respond to challenges associated with inequalities across the county.


The Northumberland Joint Strategic Needs Assessment highlights that : • Currently 26% of Northumberland's residents are aged 65, by 2043 33% of the population will be aged 65 and over. This is considerably higher than national averages. • Inequality - “Residents in our most deprived communities have an average life expectancy of 75 years compared to 87 years in the least deprived. There is a 17-year age gap in good health (healthy life expectancy) between those living in the least deprived areas and those living in the most deprived communities; 70 years of living in good health compared to 53 years ”. NCC already works hard to target inequality in Northumberland, and to support the health and wellbeing of Northumberland's residents (Northumberland joint health and wellbeing strategy 2018-2028, and NCC-Inequalities-Plan.pdf). There are many policies, projects and programmes delivered and or supported by NCC which help to reduce inequalities and improve the health and wellbeing, and thus the resilience of Northumberland's residents by reducing vulnerability and exposure to risks. For example: • The introduction of integrated impact assessments for all council activities - will help decision makers to give due regard to whether decisions reduce or widen inequalities, support net zero, protect the environment and adapt to climate change. • NCCs first Air Quality Statement - actions to keep the air quality in Northumberland good, and better communicate the risks from poor indoor air quality. • Communities First - supporting the voluntary sector in Northumberland/ • All works being delivered under the Environment policy • The Warmer Homes programme - delivering domestic energy efficiency in homes across Northumberland (funded through a variety of government grant schemes) these projects support, but are not limited to, homes most at risk of fuel poverty, and residents with health or age-based vulnerabilities. This helps households both mitigate against and adapt to a changing climate, while also reducing inequalities.


NCC are also currently undertaking a climate change risk assessment which will help support business continuity and our ability to continue to deliver essential services for residents into the future. Urban flooding and more intense storms are already affecting the District, brought by more frequent and intense heavy rain events. 

In September 2020, a surprisingly intense storm dumped almost three inches of stormwater on the District in a two hour period that overwhelmed sewer and stormwater infrastructure and led to dangerous flooding and prompted numerous rescue operations. Lyme disease and West Nile Virus are more prevalent in Toronto in part due to a gradually warming climate (not heat waves), resulting in more breeding cycles of the insect vectors. West Nile virus is thought to be more efficiently transmitted by mosquitoes to humans at higher ambient air temperatures. 
In Ontario, the blacklegged tick is the only type of tick that can transmit the bacteria that causes Lyme Disease (opens in new window).

Tick populations are expanding in Canada. Blacklegged ticks have been found in Toronto, and are established here. All of Toronto is considered an Estimated Risk Area according to Public Health Ontario's (PHO): Ontario Blacklegged Tick Established Risk Areas Map 2024. (opens in new window) Estimated risk areas are locations where blacklegged ticks have been identified or are known to occur and where humans have the potential to come into contact with infective ticks.

The risk of contracting Lyme disease in Toronto, is considered to be low but has been increasing. The risk of Lyme disease can be decreased by preventing tick bites, early detection and removal of ticks

The Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) provides information on the prevention and risks of Lyme disease (opens in new window). The 2021 Lyme disease surveillance infographic (opens in new window) provides a summary of Lyme disease cases reported in 2021 across Canada.

In November 2023, the Board of Health adopted Item 2023.HL8.3 Public Health Impacts of Climate Change in Toronto: A Path Forward for Responding to the Climate Crisis, re-establishing a commitment to leadership and collaboration on climate change and health actions that reduce health inequities. The Board of Health also recommended that the Medical Officer of Health report back in 2025 on progress on a surveillance framework, climate change health indicators, and collaboration efforts.

The most recent Toronto climate projections reinforce the need for a systematic way to track the health impacts of the increasing heat, variable precipitation and unpredictable weather that will affect health. Timely monitoring and surveillance of impacts on health and wellbeing, including from climate change, are a strategic priority action for Toronto Public Health (TPH). 

This report describes Toronto Public Health's approach to creating a climate change-related health impact surveillance framework, which will be developed over the next several years. The first phase of this work will create a publicly accessible dashboard that is expected to launch in spring 2026. The dashboard will be updated annually and will share information related to the health impacts of climate change, including:

- Heat related illnesses
- Vector borne diseases from ticks and mosquitoes
- Injuries following severe weather
- Health impacts of poor air quality
- Impacts from UV radiation
- Food-borne diseases; and
- Water quality implications.

column20: With the increase in climate change-related extreme weather events, increased UV radiation or longer vegetation periods, the risk of human health being affected is also rising. Extreme weather events such as summer heat, storms, heavy rain or floods can lead to physical damage and even to the need for care or death. In addition, the resulting physical, financial and social consequences can also cause psychological stress. Increasingly high daytime temperatures during the summer months, accompanied by little cooling at night, can put a great strain on the cardiovascular system. Increased UV exposure can promote an increase in skin cancers and is seen as a risk factor for the development of cataracts (clouding of the lens of the eye). In addition, high temperatures lead to a warming of surface waters, where they can promote the growth of microorganisms that are hazardous to health. Due to the general warming trend, the vegetation period has also extended, especially in recent years. As a result, the flowering period of individual plants has shifted or lengthened, which leads to a higher burden for those affected by pollen allergies. The increase in temperature also favours the settlement and spread of heat-loving plants and animals. For example, the alien Ambrosia plant can come into flower and release highly allergenic pollen well into the autumn. Likewise, a spread of native and non-native animals that can be vectors of pathogens, such as ticks and mosquitoes, can be observed. As a result of heavy rainfall events, surface inputs and overflows from the combined sewer system can lead to contamination of surface waters and a reduction in bathing water quality. Moisture damage in living spaces can trigger mould growth and thus cause respiratory diseases and allergies.(Source: BEK)

column20: En Bogotá, la capital de Colombia, el entendimiento y la respuesta al cambio climático han estado íntimamente ligados al crecimiento urbano acelerado y el aumento de la población. Estos factores, junto con otros determinantes de salud, han incrementado la vulnerabilidad y la sensibilidad de la población ante cambios ambientales. Los fenómenos exacerbados por la variabilidad climática han intensificado la frecuencia e impacto de eventos extremos, lo que ha motivado la creación de políticas ambientales y de salud dirigidas a estudiar y manejar los efectos del cambio climático. La respuesta institucional a estos desafíos en Bogotá se formalizó con la promulgación del Decreto 596 de 2011, que estableció la Política Distrital de Salud Ambiental, desarrollada mediante ocho (8) líneas de intervención, incluyendo al cambio climático como una propuesta que permite la implementación de estrategias y procesos de monitoreo, investigación, adaptación y mitigación orientadas a la disminución de los eventos en salud causados por este fenómeno en la ciudad. La implementación del Plan de Salud de Intervenciones Colectivas (PSPIC) ha sido un componente clave de esta política, dado que tiene como objetivo formular y ejecutar estrategias concertadas de adaptación y mitigación de la crisis climática, enfocándose en aspectos cruciales de salud pública como la justicia ambiental, la renovación de la Atención Primaria en Salud (APS), y los determinantes sociales de la salud. El PSPIC se alinea con los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible y la Política Pública de Acción Climática de Bogotá 2050, enmarcada en el Acuerdo 790 del 2020 que declara la emergencia climática en la ciudad. Este plan es fundamental para proteger y promover la salud de los habitantes de Bogotá frente a los impactos adversos del cambio climático, contribuyendo así a la construcción de una ciudad más resiliente y sostenible en el siglo XXI. En este contexto, la Secretaría Distrital de Salud, a través de la Subdirección de Vigilancia en Salud Pública y las Subredes Integradas de Servicios de Salud está comprometida con generar los parámetros y lineamientos para la vigilancia epidemiológica y ambiental. Este tipo de vigilancia incluye el monitoreo de eventos en salud y factores ambientales. La difusión de la información se realiza a través de documentos que exponen los hallazgos obtenidos, contribuyendo así a la toma de decisiones informada y la sensibilización pública

Extreme weather events caused by climate change can significantly affect the cardiovascular system, especially vulnerable groups such as the elderly, pregnant and children, and even cause to deaths. The increase in the number of people affected by heat waves, which is one of the extreme weather events, creates negative effects on health, causes the losses on labor productivity and income, decreases air quality and increases the risk of forest fires. Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality carries out many activities in order to reduce these negative effects. These are described below:

-Works are ongoing to provide the citizens with healthy and active living conditions and to develop sports grounds

.-Basic public services such as clean water, food, health and affordable housing are available to the public.

-Nature-based solutions such as parks, green roofs, green walls, blue infrastructure and permeable pavements are given priority in order to both reduce risks such as extreme heat, drought and flood caused by climate change, and to help increase the quality of life by protecting mental and physical health.

-Ensuring that air quality is kept at a level that will not adversely affect human health by constantly increasing green and shadow areas.

-It is aimed both to reduce emissions and to minimize health risks by creating “15-minute cities” where all residents of the city can meet most of their needs with a short walk or bike ride from their homes.

-In order to increase resistance to risks such as excessive precipitation, heat and cold weather waves caused by climate change, “Health at Home” services are strengthened and the need for personnel and vehicles for these services is increased.

-Pre-school and school-age children are given regular training on the health effects of climate change.

column20: Existen un total de 8746 establecimientos de salud en la Provincia de Lima, de los cuales el 45% (3907) se encuentran ubicados en Lima Centro, 22% (1904) en Lima norte, 21% (1894) en Lima Sur y el 12% (1041) restante en Lima Este. De los peligros identificados en el Análisis de Riesgo Climático, se concluye que el riesgo por inundaciones podría afectar al 1.2% (111) de los establecimientos de salud en la Provincia de Lima. Por el lado de los movimientos en masa el nivel de riesgo de los centros de salud varía en función de su localización y tamaño. Los centros, localizados en las laderas inestables donde la susceptibilidad a los movimientos en masa es alta y su tamaño es mayor (p.ej. centros con internamiento), manifiestan un nivel de riesgo muy alto. Por el contrario, los de menor tamaño y ubicados en la zona costera (p.ej. centros sin internamiento) poseen un menor riesgo. Según el CENEPRED el 2.3% (207), presenta un riesgo alto y el 0.8% (68) presenta un riesgo muy alto . Por otro lado, en cuanto al peligro olas de calor, los centros de salud poseen en su mayoría un riesgo “Moderado”. El motivo se debe a que en general son centros sin internamiento, por lo que se consideran centros de mediano tamaño con una vulnerabilidad moderada

column20: En 2017, la Secretaría del Medio Ambiente de la Ciudad de México, elaboró el \'Diagnóstico para conocer los impactos del cambio climático en mujeres y hombres de la Ciudad de México\'. con el propósito de conocer y analizar los impactos del cambio climático en grupos de mujeres y hombres de la ciudad, considerando sus actividades diarias, sus hábitos de uso y consumo de los recursos y servicios de la ciudad, de acuerdo al sexo, edad y grupo social al que pertenecen las personas, donde uno de los impactos evaluados fue el de la salud. Dicho documento sirvió de referencia en la elaboración de la Estrategia de Acción Climática 2021-2050 (ELAC) y el Programa de Acción Climática de la Ciudad de México 2021-2030 (PACCM).El diagnóstico observó que las mujeres perciben el cambio climático a nivel personal y familiar [mientras que los hombres lo perciben en otros grupos vulnerables]. Por ejemplo, se encontró que son ellas quienes se responsabilizan del cuidado de las familias y las comunidades ante enfermedades vinculadas con el cambio climático, generando mayores gastos económicos para atenderse a sí mismas o a personas enfermas. Incluso coinciden en que cuando se enferman por manifestaciones del clima, difícilmente son cuidadas por sus compañeros, reconociendo que el cuidado principal se los brindan otras mujeres, incluyendo familiares, amigas, vecinas, compañeras de trabajo y mujeres de edad mayor.Enlace al Diagnóstico: http://www.data.sedema.cdmx.gob.mx/cambioclimaticocdmx/images/biblioteca_cc/diagnostico-impactos_cambio_climatico.pdf\n\nEs importante mencionar que durante la elaboración y publicación de la ELAC y el PACCM, el mundo y la Ciudad de México enfrentaron uno de los mayores retos de salud pública en la era moderna. La emergencia global derivada de la pandemia por COVID-19 ha evidenciado las mayores fortalezas y fragilidades de nuestro modelo económico y social y del sistema urbano-ambiental. En este sentido se destinó un capítulo completo a la planeación climática en un futuro post covid-2019.

The municipality has established a network of neighbourhood centres that are free and open to the public during the summer. These centers provide hospitality and socialization opportunities, with a special focus on meeting the needs of the most vulnerable individuals during this season. To protect outdoor workers, the Lombardy region prohibits outdoor work from 12:30 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. during July, August, and September for at-risk workers.\n The Urban Resilience Department, working together with academic institutions and other city stakeholders, has developed a heat risk map. column20: Vectorial born diseases: As explained above, the increased importance of water and nature in cities, as part of adaptation to climate change, leads to an increased risk of tiger mosquito implantation or the stronger presence of the common mosquito. This issue is taken into account by monitoring the implantation of tiger mosquitoes on the territory and actions to suppress larval gites. Innovations such as bioclimatic mosquito nets are also being tested and assessed in public buildings.Heat-related illnesses: The increase in heat wave episodes can weaken certain categories of the population.The Heat Wave Plan provides for prevention and warning measures that concern in particular the elderly, who are more vulnerable and often more isolated, as well as children and homeless people. Registration on a file of isolated vulnerable people for monitoring during heat waves and other health risks. In addition, Parisians can search for cool places on Paris website . It lists more than 900 islands of coolness in Paris, whether permanent (gardens, municipal facilities ...) or temporary (foggers, exceptional openings of parks ...). Waters-born diseases: medical monitoring and risk prevention (vaccination against leptospirosis, taking into account the risk of heat, mosquitoes, rats, etc.) is deployed for agents working in high-risk professions (sewer workers, cleaning agents, park and gardens, etc.). In addition, a coordinated rat control plan is being implemented in Paris. Air-born diseases : the increase in temperature could also bring certain allergenic species to new regions (particularly for herbaceous plants that move more quickly), promote pollen production and make pollen more allergenic (increase in the quantities of allergens). The allergic risk associated with pollen exposure is monitored by the City and the National Aerobiological Monitoring Network (NAMN), and the results are communicated to the public and health professionals to help limit the health impact. In addition, the City's vegetalization policy takes into account the allergic risk in the choice of plant species planted.Concerning diseases related to air pollution: the 2017-2025 Air Protection Plan (APP) for Île-de-France was approved in 2018. It aims at reducing air pollution from all sectors of activity: air, agriculture, industry, residential and transportation. It particularly targets wood heating and road traffic, the main sources of fine particles and nitrogen dioxides in Ile-de-France. On the local level, several reference documents have been put in place by the City of Paris: The Parisian Health and Environment Plan (PPSE) to reduce health damage linked to the degradation of our environment, and the Paris' Climate Action Plan.

column20: The Philadelphia Department of Public Health completed an analysis of the impacts of climate change and public health in the city and found that the extreme heat, increased precipitation, and more frequent storms climate change will bring to our region will significantly impact public health. Precipitation changes and extreme storms will increase occurrences of vector- borne diseases, increase community and individual trauma associated with flooding, negatively impact health due to post-storm exposure to mold and toxins transported by floodwaters, and could lead to death or injury. Extreme heat is the most deadly climate hazard. It exacerbates many existing health conditions like asthma and cardiovascular disease and heat stress can cause injury or death, especially amongst the most vulnerable residents, including children, elderly, those with preexisting health conditions, and those living in poverty. Temperature increases also exacerbate mental health challenges and research has shown that gun violence and suicide increase during excessive heat events.

column20: Os perigos climáticos selecionados possuem uma relação, sendo direta ou indireta, com inúmeros problemas de saúde que atingem a população e o meio urbano. É necessário incentivar e promover iniciativas articuladas com outros parceiros e atores, visando prevenir e reduzir os danos da exposição da população aos riscos de saúde associados à poluição do ar, do solo, das águas, por produtos químicos e aos desastres naturais e tecnológicos no município de São Paulo. O estresse térmico, por exemplo, que é uma condição de aumento ou diminuição da temperatura no ambiente durante determinado período de tempo, provoca danos diversos para a saúde e o bem-estar da população. Quando relacionado à elevação da temperatura, contribui para o aumento de doenças relacionadas ao calor, bem como cãibras, exaustão, síncope e edema. Já o estresse térmico relacionado à redução brusca de temperatura, contribui para doenças relacionadas ao frio, que incluem gripes, resfriados, sinusite, pneumonia, dentre outros. Ainda, para o ambiente, a alteração brusca de temperatura prejudica o desenvolvimento da vegetação, o que pode representar um empecilho para a manutenção da biodiversidade na cidade.Os rios, córregos e demais cursos d'água da cidade de São Paulo, são, em geral, canalizados, impermeabilizados e soterrados. Dessa forma, estão repletos de construções urbanas acima ou em suas margens. Ademais, muitos são utilizados pelo sistema de esgoto para o despejo de dejetos, tornando-os potenciais vetores de transmissão de doenças. A ocorrência de tempestades ou precipitações intensas, pode ocasionar o transbordo da água dos rios, tornando a população mais suscetível à contaminação e, assim, à doenças e infecções. \nPor fim, a perda de espaços e cobertura verdes na cidade estão diretamente relacionadas com a perda de qualidade de vida e bem-estar da população. Estudos indicam que o contato com ambientes verdes contribuem para a saúde mental, melhorando o humor e reduzindo sintomas de doenças mentais como depressão e ansiedade. O estudo em questão pode ser verificado no link: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-44097-3 * Os prazos para o impacto incluem curto, médio e longo prazo.

It has been documented (http://www.futuredirections.org.au/publication/climate-change-and-australian-food-security/ and https://www.climatecouncil.org.au/uploads/7579c324216d1e76e8a50095aac45d66.pdf ) that Australia's agriculture industry and food supply chain (and therefore food availability) has suffered and will continue to suffer as Australia's climate continues to change - especially due to rising temperatures, lower rainfall and increases in severe weather events. Already there are a lot of people experiencing food security issues due to low-income and a range of other factors. These issues will be exacerbated by climate change. If drought and mismanagement of water change the agricultural sector and ability to grow food there will be issues of food security - which typically affects those with lower incomes as food prices will increase. The impact for City of Adelaide is not specifically documented, and nor does the City have a plan for addressing the issues of food security in a changing climate, or food security more generally. 

In April 2024, the South Australian state government released a paper on Food Secure Communities in South Australia. As part of this paper, they identified that 16% of people surveyed in a South Australian survey reported being food insecure (with or without hunger). Broader Australian data also identified that for many people, food insecurity is a long-term issue (i.e. longer than 1 year). A rapid evidence review, Food Secure Communities in South Australia - An evidence summary to support food security across food and social systems was prepared by independent experts to help understand what equitable, sustainable, nutritious and secure food systems look like and what SA can learn from these models. The evidence review identified potential actions across SA to improve food access, availability, utilisation, agency, sustainability and stability. On release of this paper, the SA government undertook a survey of residents to identify lived experiences of food insecurity, how they have impacted the community and what the community believes could and should be done to address this. The outcomes of this survey are yet to be released and City of Adelaide will review the results when they are to identify any alignment with actions that can be undertaken at a local level.
A 2024 Report from Foodbank (https://reports.foodbank.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/2024_Foodbank_Hunger_Report_IPSOS-Report.pdf) stated that around 32% of Australian's had experienced severe (19%) or moderate food insecurity in the past 12 months.

SA Health has recognised the additional burden that climate change is already placing on the South Australian Health system, and will increase. It has a released a 'Climate Change and Health Framework 2025 - 2030' which covers metropolitan Adelaide. The Framework recognises that the health system has already experienced damage to healthcare infrastructure, impacts to population health, increasing patient presentations, increasing infectious disease outbreaks, and impacts on workforce.

The mission of the Framework is the 'Transformation of the South Australian Government's health system through reducing environmental impact, achieving net zero emissions, and adapting to current and future impacts of climate change at scale and at pace, in an equitable way.'

The framework has 4 goals including:

1. Environmentally responsible
2. Net Zero in all areas of operations, service delivery and culture
3. Climate-resilient to the impacts of climate change
4. Provider of high-quality health services for patients and communities

Beyond the SA Health Framework, key climate related concerns that will need to be investigated for our health system include: 
•Future-proofing hospitals to filter out smoke •Increasing messaging to more vulnerable members of community and workforces 
•Message fatigue - the need to communicate simply about a vast range of health topics means we don't always hit the mark or people don't notice it anymore

In relation to 'Health-related risk and vulnerability assessment undertaken' - yes was ticked because various vulnerability assessments have been undertaken for Adelaide and South Australia in relation to heat by SA Health at a statewide level. 

Health impacts from heat: 
The increase in the incidence of heatwaves and extreme heat is expected to continue to adversely impact the health, safety and wellbeing of vulnerable members of the community. These include members of the community who are already vulnerable due to poor mental or physical health, the elderly, those who are isolated by a lack of mobility or transport options and/or are highly dependent on particular facilities or support. The risk factors and vulnerabilities for heat related illnesses also increase during a heatwave for those who work outdoors, can't get access to cooling overnight, or who suffer mental illnesses and exacerbates Non-Communicable Disease Symptoms (e.g. respiratory disease, cardiovascular disease, renal disease). It is hard to specifically account for deaths and presentations to extreme heat or heatwaves, as these can impact existing medical conditions which is what they are presenting with. 

Low socio economic households: 
A barrier to keeping cool during extreme heat and heatwaves is the cost and ability to cool down homes. The cost of utilities to a household fluctuates seasonally and can cause bill shock if air-conditioning and water costs increase over summer in order to remain safe. Others might not turn on their air-conditioners or don't have one, which may increase their risk-factors especially if elderly or with pre-existing health conditions. 56.5% of the CoA population is renting - made up of 6.4% social housing and 49.9% private. Renters typically have a lower income and have limited ability to alter the thermal comfort of their home and lower bills - for example affording energy efficient technologies and upgrades. 

Wildlife:
In 2010 the nationally threatened Grey-headed Flying-fox (GHFF) species established a campsite in the Adelaide Park Lands, one factor to their migration pattern could be climate change. Some flying foxes carry diseases, including Australian bat lyssavirus and the Hendra virus - which are only transmittable if a person is bitten or scratched. Temperatures higher than 42°C can kill the flying-foxes, and mass cleanups cause health hazards over multiple days - health hazards for the public at risk of coming into contact with them, and for the vaccinated workers and volunteers active in the days of extreme heat to rescue bats and clean up carcasses. The CoA has worked extensively with partner organisations to developed management plans and practices to address the GHFF issue successfully. 

Air pollution: 
Like all cities, the CoA suffers from air quality issues associated with density of fuel-based transportation and other factors, including pollen, bushfires and dust. Over the summer of 2020/21 various regions in South Australia including the Adelaide Hills, east of the CoA, experienced extreme bushfires which resulted in smoke blanketing the city on some days and impacted workers who lived or had to travel through these areas. 

Mental health: There has generally been an increase of mental health issues associated with 'eco-anxiety' or the state of the planet. Mental health issues are and will continue to increase with the displacement and loss that surrounds natural disasters such as prolonged drought, floods and bushfires. 

Rough sleepers (Information from Adelaide Zero Project Monthly Dashboard for May 2025): 
The CoA currently has 183 people sleeping rough with and a further 26 in temporary accommodation and 5 other actively homeless status unknown. We know that approximately 66.9% of rough sleepers have physical health issues, 83.4% suffer from ill mental health and 66.2% are struggling with substance abuse. Nearly half have a combination of all three (trimorbidity). This places them at much higher risk in extreme weather conditions than the general population with an often-impaired capacity for appropriate self-care and less opportunity to shelter from the elements.

column20: Heat is the leading weather-related cause of death in the United States. Although Maine is not expected to see the same extreme temperatures as other parts of the country, the impact of a high heat day or a heat wave has a very different impact depending on the region and time of the year. Unseasonably hot days, extreme heat, as well as extended heat waves can have a significant physiological impact on people whose bodies are less acclimated to warmer weather, which both affects people in historically cooler climates and makes extreme temperatures in the spring more deadly than those later in the summer. Likewise, air conditioning is much less prevalent in homes, businesses, and public spaces in Portland. Both due to human physiology and due to infrastructural cooling capacity, cities in cooler climates like Portland tend to see more heat-related deaths and hospitalizations. Health issues from extreme heat can lead to heat exhaustion, heat stroke, and hyperthermia. Prolonged exposure to heat also exacerbates asthma, heart disease, and diabetes, leading to more hospitalizations for kidney, cardiovascular, and respiratory disorders. A string of days that also have high minimum temperatures prevents bodies from being able to recover, amplifying the health risk. Residents who live and work in areas with more impervious surfaces and less green space will likely feel high heat more acutely. Areas with a significant portion of impervious surfaces, which includes many of Portland's socially vulnerable neighborhoods, will likely feel hotter due to higher surface temperatures. Residents who work in outdoor occupations, will have greater vulnerability to periods of high heat. Children, older adults, residents with disabilities, and residents without access to air conditioning will also be more vulnerable. There are fourteen vector-borne diseases of concern in the United States, and nine of those diseases (two mosquito-borne and seven tick-borne) have been identified in Maine. Lyme disease is the primary and most common vector-borne disease in Maine as of 2019. Symptoms for Lyme disease in humans usually include a fever, headache, fatigue, and a skin rash called erythema migraines. If left untreated, the infection can spread, resulting in chronic joint pain and neurological dysfunction. Changes in the climate, including warmer winters, higher humidity, and more precipitation, impact the breeding and survival rates of ticks and mosquitoes, as well as the reproductive rate of the pathogens. Rates of Lyme disease have increased significantly in the past couple decades from less than 100 reported cases in 2000 to 1,373 reported cases in 2018 (280 of which were in Portland's Cumberland County). Major storms, including associated heavy precipitation, high winds, and flooding, bring a wide range of health and safety risks. Most directly, these climate hazards lead to injuries and fatalities due to drowning; blunt injuries from falling objects or debris moving in floodwater currents; electrocution from exposure to electrical systems and electric shocks transmitted through flood waters; as well as vehicle accidents due to slick, eroded, or obstructed roadways. Impaired infrastructure and building damage can likewise lead to cascading health risks through loss or disruption in electricity/power, transportation, communication, and water and sanitation systems. All of these factors create heightened health risks, which can be amplified by an inability to access medical care, medical equipment, or medications. For example, compromised road and transportation systems restrict access for first responders, and limit access to medical care. Loss of refrigeration—at residential, commercial, and industrial scales—also can compromise food safety and lead to foodborne illnesses. Likewise, waterborne illness is a major concern. A large number of studies now show that climate change will likely exacerbate poor air quality over time. Ozone at ground level can cause significant public health concerns by causing inflammation in the lungs. This inflammation leads to coughing and throat irritation in the short-term; over the long-term, lung tissues become less elastic, more sensitive to allergens, and more prone to infections—often leading to chronic conditions like asthma. Changes in meteorological factors such as higher humidity and stagnation could also lead to higher levels of particulate matter, which has shown to trigger cardiovascular problems The health effects of climate change are not only physical, but also mental and emotional. They stem from the immediate trauma from a local climate-related event; from the ongoing emotional toll of processing information about climate change and its consequences; and from stress induced by witnessing changes in the environment and a loss of a sense of place or identity.

column20: Increased heat waves are the most important climate-related change for human health. The risk of cardiovascular problems, heat stroke, dehydration and hyperthermia is increasing. The elderly, the (chronically) sick and those in need of care, as well as pregnant women, infants and small children are particularly sensitive. Extreme events such as floods and severe storms can result in injuries and deaths. Such events can also have serious psychological consequences. A negative impact of heat waves on work productivity and sleep quality can affect the well-being of the entire population. The pollen season and thus the exposure time for allergy sufferers will be longer. People with pollen allergies are also particularly affected by the spread of invasive plants, such as the highly allergenic ragweed. The tiger mosquito and the Asian bush mosquito have already established themselves as new disease vectors. Ticks are also expected to continue spreading. While a decrease is expected for tick-borne encephalitis due to the heat sensitivity of the viruses, the risk of borreliosis remains. Other possible indirect effects on human health can be triggered by longer periods of drought, the changing rainfall regime and the floods. These altered hazards and effects can have an impact on the water regime and thus on drinking water quality.

column20:
Os debates sobre o meio ambiente e a saúde global não são mais separados, pois os sistemas de suporte à vida estão começando a ruir como resultado da escala das atividades humanas. A escala do padrão de consumo global excede a capacidade do planeta de absorver os
resíduos que produzimos ou de oferecer de forma sustentável os recursos que usamos. Isso está afetando a qualidade e a quantidade de comida que produzimos, a qualidade do ar e da água, a exposição a eventos climáticos extremos, a exposição a doenças infecciosas, episódios como a pandemia, e até a habitabilidade de alguns dos locais onde vivemos.
As mudanças climáticas em Belo Horizonte agravam a saúde pública, com a intensificação de casos de insolação e desidratação pelo calor extremo; aumento de doença tropicais com as temperaturas elevadas e precipitação intensa e irregular; aumento e intensificação de episódios prolongados de baixa umidade do ar e poluição que ampliam quadros respiratórios; aumento de doenças cardiovasculares devido ao estresse térmico. 
Esses impactos afetam a saúde principalmente da população mais vulnerável, porque a desigualdade social e vulnerabilidade climática torna esses grupos mais suscetíveis às mudanças climáticas, o que demanda mais proteção, com ampliação e acesso à saúde pública e de políticas de adaptação urbana inclusivas. 
O município de Belo Horizonte tem intensificado a sua Política de Enfrentamento às Mudanças Climáticas alinhado com a saúde da população e com planos e programas que consideram o cenário das mudanças climáticas. O Plano Local de Ação Climática (PLAC-BH) e o Plano de Redução das Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (PREGEE-BH) traçam ações para a promoção da redução de emissões de GEE, incentivo à energia limpa a arborização urbana que reduzem as ilhas de calor e melhoram a qualidade do ar na cidade. O Plano Municipal de Arborização Urbana (PMAU-BH) prevê a ampliação e manejo qualificado da cobertura arbórea da cidade, contribuindo com a melhoria da qualidade do ar e sombreamento, reduzindo as doenças relacionadas ao calor extremo. Os Refúgios Climáticos são espaços de resfriamento com sombreamento e disponibilidade gratuíta de água potável para consumo que auxilia nos efeitos provocados pelas mudanças do clima na saúde da população, funcionando como um 'oásis urbano' na cidade. A Defesa Civil de Belo Horizonte conta com um sistema de alertas e monitoramento nowcasting que amplia o olhar operacional sobre o comportamento da atmosfera que informa à população informações meteorológicas importantes como a presença do fenômeno de Ondas de Calor, baixa umidade do ar, surto de doenças epidemiológicas, temperaturas baixas, possibilidade de chuvas intensas e vias bloqueadas. Atualmente, o município também conta com o Protocolo de Calor que está em fase de elaboração, e que auxiliará na redução dos impactos à saúde da população e nos cuidados especiais para os grupos vulneráveis.

column20: In Baltimore, the number of days when temperatures reach or exceed 90°F are projected to increase to between 35 and 38 days by 2050, and between 38 and 41 days a year by the end of the century. Similarly, according to the National Climate Assessment, regional climate model simulations suggest that Maryland could experience more than twice as many days per year over 95°F by midcentury— with an estimated 15 additional days above 95°F each year. This is expected to severely impact vulnerable populations, infrastructure, agriculture and ecosystems. In the future, Baltimore expects that periods of extreme heat are likely to increase in frequency, duration, and intensity. The summer season in Baltimore City is known to have frequent high temperatures accompanied by high humidity. On some summer days, urban air can reach temperatures up to 10°F warmer than that of surrounding suburban or rural areas—a phenomenon known as the “urban heat island effect.” Densely developed metropolitan areas tend to replace natural land cover with asphalt, sidewalks, buildings, and other hard infrastructure. As opposed to natural elements of an ecosystem, which can absorb the sun's heat and cool the surrounding air through evapotranspiration, these hard materials retain and radiate heat. The resulting warm urban temperatures can give rise to adverse public and environmental health problems and can increase energy usage for summertime cooling. The urban heat island effect is anticipated to intensify as extreme heat events increase as a result of climate change.A significant increase in the number of extreme heat days could place people at even greater risk of suffering from heat-related health conditions, including heat stress, heat exhaustion, or heat stroke. In addition to urban agriculture and tree canopy, surface water supplies are susceptible to 
severe impacts from drought. Baltimore City DPW stores potable water in three surface 
reservoirs: Prettyboy, Lock Raven, and Liberty. These reservoirs house 86 billion gallons of 
potable water to supply 1.8 million people living in Baltimore City and Anne Arundel, 
Baltimore, Carroll, and Howard Counties (Baltimore City Department of Public Works n.d.).

(MDE) performs monthly monitoring of precipitation, stream flow, groundwater levels, and reservoir storage. At full capacity, the three City reservoirs can provide potable water for 
approximately 350 days (Maryland Department of the Environment 2021). Drought can result

The health risks of climate change have been identified as an area of particular concern for Cape Town. Cape Town has a baseline of poor health in general, with high levels of HIV/AIDS and TB infection as well as high levels of non-communicable diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease. Although health care is provided for free or at minimal cost at government facilities (as well as at high cost in private facilities), these facilities - including infrastructure, service delivery, staff and overall capacity - are vulnerable to being impacted by and overwhelmed by high demand and the knock-on effects due to a disease outbreak or extreme weather events. The City of Cape Town is currently part of a project lead by the University of Cape Town (UCT) called “Cascading Climate and Health Risks in African Cities” (CASCADE). A Memorandum of Agreement to contribute to an improved working relationship between the City and UCT on various collaborative projects, including CASCADE, is currently being finalised. The project aims to advance the understanding of critical urban health challenges faced by African cities that will inform practical and effective planning and interventions at a local government level. Since project inception in 2023, CASCADE has implemented two learning labs, collaborated with partner universities to share lessons and continued research activities Partner institutes include: The Climate System Analysis Group (CSAG), University of Cape Town; Global Change Institute, University of Witwatersrand; Infectious Diseases Institute, Makerere University; University of Ghana; Chinhoyi University of Technology; Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre; START International; African Population and Health Research Centre 

https://www.csag.uct.ac.za/2024/04/09/getting-to-know-cascade/ 

https://www.cascade.org.za/ 
The Climate Change Risk and Vulnerability Assessment developed for the City of Cape Town Metropolitan District Health Sector in 2021, reflect the climate change risks identified for the City and the anticipated vulnerabilities for the Health Sector and the communities that they serve including shifts in experiences of particular diseases (increase or decrease of prevalence, shift in geographical presence), damage to services or insufficient capacity of health services to respond to health care needs. The risks and vulnerabilities of the report are informed by projections based on models of potential climate change exposures and assumptions at the time of writing the report, relevant literature and professional opinions of the health sector implications, with a 2050 horizon, and baseline data of Burden of Disease (BoD) in 2019-2020,The climate change data used is from the CSIR's Greenbook, a climate change dataset developed for use by national, provincial, and local government, the Climate Research Unit's Timeseries climate change data, and a dataset developed by OneWorld.

Climate hazards can become a threat multiplier through impacts on sectors that are essential for service delivery such as water and electricity access and supply and waste management, as well as sectors that contribute to the health and wellbeing of the public such as food systems and the food value chain, and access to recreational facilities and services which contributes to mental and physical wellbeing and health. Impacts on critical infrastructure located in vulnerable locations such as heat island risk areas, areas that are frequently flooded, or frequently impacted by strong winds and storms - can cause limited access to water and electricity. This is a concern especially for health facilities and in areas with existing service delivery challenges can greatly contribute to exacerbating health challenges or limit the capacity at which health services can be provided. Climate hazards can also cause disruption to waste management services and increase health challenges form inadequate waste management practices in areas experiencing existing challenges. The impacts of climate hazards on food systems will primarily affect the food value chain during the agricultural production phase, as well as cold storage and transportation for exports and local distribution. Impacts also include risks to the quality of food sold by street vendors and at open-air markets, and how people access food at informal markets and larger commercial shops. 

To address these risks, the City is in the process of developing new health indicators through the Urban Health Programme and Monitoring Initiative which forms part of a global network of 73 cities. The programme will enable the City to understand the underlying causes of health issues such as service delivery challenges and access to services and spaces. The indicators will help the City to identify relevant interventions, and track and evaluate these actions. To inform the implementation of this programme, the City developed an urban health framework tailored specifically to Cape Town's unique burden of disease, inequalities and natural disaster vulnerabilities. This was achieved through a process that includes the review of existing literature on urban health and urban health frameworks, identifying key determinants, linking suitable indicators to each determinant, and engaging city officials to ensure the framework's practical implementation. The scoping review was conducted to source and appraise relevant literature for conceptualising and monitoring urban health in settings with similar socio-economic and spatial dynamics to the City of Cape Town. The scoping review pivoted on the following central research question: “What are the existing approaches and/or activities linked to the monitoring of urban health in settings similar to Cape Town?”, which guided the search terms used to retrieve scientific and grey literature from Google Scholar™ and Google™. Relevant studies were selected based on pre-defined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The final list of literature was analysed to gain a broad overview of the field and identify key theories, concepts, and indicators used in existing frameworks. Following the scoping review, the draft conceptual framework and served as a preliminary model for the City's unique urban health context, drawing upon the insights gathered from the review. Afectaciones, cambio de dinámicas y grupos vulnerables ante las olas de calor: Los problemas para dormir siguen siendo la principal afectación reportada en 2024 con un 57.5%, por debajo del 61.6% reportado en 2023.

La población más vulnerable frente a los efectos del cambio climático es la que habita en el área metropolitana de Guadalajara. 
'La mortalidad por enfermedades cardiovasculares muestra la mayor correlación con las temperaturas máximas extremas.
La mayor significancia estadística con el peligro de las temperaturas máximas se presentó para la morbilidad por enfermedades transmisibles consideradas por la Secretaría de Salud como Infecciones intestinales por otros organismos y las mal definidas que incluyen las infecciones

Certain populations face heightened vulnerabilities during hurricanes, with one key area of concern being low-income individuals and families living in older or lower-quality housing. These structures often lack the necessary resilience to withstand severe weather events, such as storm impact-resistant windows, reinforced doors, or adequate roofing. As a result, residents may be unable to shelter in place during a storm, increasing their risk of injury, displacement, or exposure to hazardous conditions. 

In addition to structural vulnerabilities, extended power outages commonly occur after storms, posing significant health risks, especially for women, children, and the elderly. These groups are particularly susceptible to heat-related illnesses in homes without air conditioning (A/C) or proper ventilation. This risk is exacerbated in areas with limited access to backup power sources or emergency cooling centers. 

Furthermore, the lack of adequate health services during and after a storm can also increase health risks. Communities with limited access to healthcare facilities may struggle to receive critical medical attention during emergencies, further compounding the public health impacts of hurricanes. Addressing these vulnerabilities requires enhanced preparedness, such as ensuring access to cooling centers, strengthening shelter-in-place protocols, and improving access to emergency medical care, particularly for vulnerable populations.

This water often contains harmful objects, chemical pollutants, and organic contaminants, such as fecal matter from pets or septic systems. Additionally, standing water creates an ideal breeding ground for mosquitoes, increasing the risk of vector-borne diseases like Zika and West Nile virus. 

Flooding in homes and vehicles caused by rainstorms and King Tides can lead to the growth of mold, which not only causes property damage but also poses serious health hazards, particularly for individuals with respiratory conditions or weakened immune systems. 

These health risks are exacerbated by climate change, as more frequent and intense storms and higher tides increase the likelihood of exposure to polluted floodwater. In the City of Miami, a hotter, wetter climate is projected to extend the mosquito season, increasing the potential for the transmission of vector-borne diseases such as Zika virus, dengue, and West Nile virus. These conditions create an environment where disease-carrying mosquitoes can thrive for longer periods and spread more widely throughout the community. 

The City was a hotspot for Zika virus transmission in 2016, highlighting the community's vulnerability to mosquito-borne outbreaks. Without proactive community participation, particularly in managing standing water around homes and neighborhoods, there will remain an ongoing risk of future epidemics. 

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) specifically recommends that pregnant individuals take precautions to reduce exposure to mosquito bites, as Zika virus is of particular concern during pregnancy. It can be transmitted from mother to fetus and is linked to serious birth defects. 

To better understand and prepare for these emerging health threats, climate models are used to project future scenarios specific to the City. These models take into account trends such as rising temperatures, precipitation patterns, and sea-level rise, providing valuable data to guide public health planning and interventions. By strengthening vector control, improving flood management, enhancing sanitation systems, and expanding health surveillance and early warning systems, Miami can mitigate these health risks and protect its residents from the evolving threats posed by climate change.

Extreme heat is a major threat in the U.S., particularly in cities like Miami. Marginalized communities, often low-income or communities of color, face heightened risks due to hotter neighborhoods and limited resources for protection. The lack of air conditioning in these communities leaves vulnerable individuals particularly susceptible to heat-related illnesses. Low-income workers, including pregnant individuals, also require accommodations in hot conditions to avoid heat stress. 

Days with a heat index above 105°F endanger all Miami residents, with heat-related issues such as cramps, exhaustion, heatstroke, and, in severe cases, death. During extreme heat, the body works overtime to maintain a normal temperature, which can exacerbate existing health conditions. 

Specific Vulnerable Groups: 

Pregnant People: Exposure to high temperatures during pregnancy has been linked to premature birth, low birth weight, and stillbirth. Pregnant individuals are also more susceptible to heat stress. 

Babies and Children: Babies have limited ability to regulate their body temperature, making them especially vulnerable to heat-related illnesses. Children may not recognize thirst or dehydration promptly and should avoid prolonged outdoor play, particularly in the summer. According to 2023 Census data, 4.2% of City residents are under the age of 5. 

Older Adults: Older adults face a higher risk of death during heatwaves and are more susceptible to heat-related illnesses. According to 2023 Census data, 15.9% of City residents are over the age of 65. 

People with Health Conditions: Individuals with circulatory or respiratory conditions, as well as those who are overweight, are at greater risk of heat-related illnesses. 

Outdoor Workers: Miami's rapid growth and ongoing construction projects expose many workers to heat stress. Construction workers, in particular, are at risk for heat-related illnesses while working outdoors. 

Individuals with Mental Health Conditions: Prolonged exposure to high temperatures can increase stress, anxiety, and exacerbate existing mental health conditions. Certain medications, including antidepressants, can impair the body's ability to regulate temperature, raising the risk of heat-related illnesses or death. 

CAPA Strategies' Heat Watch program focuses on understanding the health impacts of extreme heat in urban areas. Using mobile sensors, the program maps ambient air temperatures across the region with a high level of detail (10-meter granularity). This high-resolution mapping helps identify heat hotspots and variations in temperature throughout the day. By comparing heat levels with physical and social variables, the program generates datasets that can inform heat planning and response strategies. 

Climate models are also used to project future scenarios specific to Miami, taking into account factors such as rising temperatures, changes in precipitation patterns, and sea-level rise. These projections help anticipate the potential health impacts of extreme heat, including increased heat stress and the spread of vector-borne diseases.

A Secretaria de Saúde do Recife reconhece que, atualmente, ainda não dispõe de meios adequados para medir de forma precisa os impactos das mudanças climáticas sobre a saúde da população. Persistem limitações operacionais, técnicas e estruturais que dificultam o avanço nessa agenda.

No momento, o município não conta com indicadores de saúde específicos para monitorar efeitos climáticos, tampouco com séries históricas consolidadas que permitam identificar tendências, padrões sazonais ou atribuir causalidade entre eventos climáticos e agravos. Soma-se a isso a ausência de sistemas de monitoramento contínuo, modelagem preditiva e análises epidemiológicas estruturadas que integrem dados ambientais, sociais e sanitários.

É importante destacar que os impactos das mudanças climáticas se manifestam de forma indireta, multifatorial e profundamente influenciada pelos determinantes sociais da saúde. Essa complexidade exige ferramentas analíticas mais avançadas, interoperabilidade entre sistemas e equipes capacitadas — recursos que ainda estão em processo de desenvolvimento no âmbito municipal.

Apesar dessas limitações, o Recife reconhece a relevância estratégica do tema e encontra-se em processo de fortalecimento institucional. Estão sendo estruturadas ações para aprimorar a vigilância, qualificar bases de dados, implementar indicadores sensíveis ao clima e criar condições para que, no futuro, o município possa realizar monitoramento e avaliações mais precisas, apoiando políticas públicas eficazes de adaptação e mitigação.
