column20: The Maricopa County Environmental Services Department is the agency for the region with the primary responsibility for addressing vector-borne diseases (VBD). The threat of VBD is an emerging climate change concern in Phoenix. New and increased disease risks means more urgency for community and public service agencies to manage and adapt to these environmental challenges. Mosquito-borne diseases are the most common VBD reported in Maricopa County and Phoenix. Mosquitoes, like other vectors, are sensitive to changes in climate. The Maricopa County Environmental Services Office of Vector Control tests for several VBD, including West Nile virus, St. Louis Encephalitis, and Dengue, among others. In 2022, the Maricopa County Department of Public Health reported two cases of locally acquired Dengue, the first in the area unrelated to travel. Phoenix established the Office of Public Health in October 2022. The Office of Public Health has identified several objectives with Maricopa County to address and reduce VBD. The City provides information and resources to residents, businesses, and decision-makers to avoid infection and to reduce the risk of infection from VBD. Phoenix works across City departments to develop strategies, policies, and practices that reduce community exposure to VBD through vector control measures such as reducing and removing standing water. The City works to increase community and employee awareness of VBD, risks, and response plans through public service announcements and direct education and training.

column20: In 2024, Maricopa County recorded 608 heat-associated deaths according to recent reports. This count represents a 5.7% decrease in confirmed heat-related mortality compared to 2023 (https://www.maricopa.gov/ArchiveCenter/ViewFile/Item/5934). Specific to the City of Phoenix, there were 337 heat-related deaths in 2024. Approximately 60% of Maricopa County heat-associated deaths occurred among individuals aged 50 years or older. 77% of all heat-associated deaths in 2024 occurred outdoors. In recent years, people experiencing homelessness have accounted for an increasingly large share of all heat-associated deaths. Phoenix continues to act as a major partner in the Maricopa County Heat Relief Network. This network has over 60 facilities participating in 2025 and offers cooling centers as well as hydration stations. The City has added extended hours, overnight capacity, and professional navigation services at several of its Heat Relief Network locations. During 2025, a dedicated heat respite and navigation space is available at Jackson St in a large warehouse space 24 hours per day, every day of the week; Harmon, Cholla, and Yucca Libraries remain open as cooling centers with dedicated staffing until 10 pm every day of the week. The City's 2025 Heat Response Plan, updated annually, was presented to and approved by the Phoenix City Council in March 2025 (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/heat-news/city-of-phoenix-opens-heat-relief-locations-to-keep-residents-sa.html). This plan outlines 30 actions across eight strategy areas that the City leads and coordinates to protect the public from adverse heat health outcomes. Phoenix created 370 new shelter beds in 2024. An additional 310 shelter beds have opened so far in 2025, with an additional 70 beds planned to open by the end of 2025. In 2024, Phoenix implemented a data-driven pilot program to increase equitable access to chilled drinking water in public spaces. The five fountains in this initiative have delivered more than 130,000 average-size plastic bottles of water to residents from July 2024 to April 2025. Phoenix has 7 fountains installed as of summer 2025. (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/innovation/chilled-drinking-water-initiative.html)

column20: Phoenix has significant challenges with air pollution, but does not have regulatory jurisdiction over air pollution sources. Phoenix's local air quality regulator is the Maricopa County Department of Air Quality and the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality. Some uncertainty exists for Maricopa County regarding ozone and PM2.5. Maricopa County has been in moderate nonattainment for the 2015 ozone standard and was expected to move to serious nonattainment in 2025 after not meeting the standard by the required deadline. However, this downgrade has been paused, and Maricopa County is now expected to remain in moderate nonattainment pending approval of an updated Moderate Area Plan. The revised plan is expected to be submitted to EPA in fall 2025 and will include the additions of impacts from international transport emissions (CAA 179B demonstration) and should endeavor to account for the impact of wildfires on ozone concentrations. The EPA reduced the air quality standard for the allowable annual concentration of PM2.5 in February 2024. Maricopa County does not meet attainment for PM2.5 when evaluated against the new standard; however, a draft nonattainment boundary has not been submitted to the EPA by Arizona's governor. Maricopa County is currently in serious nonattainment for PM10. Maricopa County is in maintenance for carbon monoxide after being in serious nonattainment from 1992 to 2004. Maricopa County currently meets and exceeds the EPA standards for the criteria air pollutants NO2, Pb, and SO2. Phoenix partners with other governmental entities, including Maricopa County Air Quality Department (MCAQD), Arizona Department of Environmental Quality (ADEQ), and Maricopa Association of Governments (MAG) to meet these standards and maintain real-time monitoring and emission inventories. In 2022, Phoenix became a Signatory City of the C40 Clean Air Cities Declaration, which requires Phoenix to report progress updates to C40's Clean Air Accelerator. The 2023 report included setting baseline levels for air pollutants and reduction targets and updates on new polices and top pollution-reducing actions. The full report can be found online at https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/cdp/Phoenix%20C40_Clean_Air_Accelerator.pdf. As a major employer, Maricopa County Ordinance P-7 requires the City of Phoenix to develop, implement, and maintain a Travel Reduction Program (TRP) to reduce air emissions related to employee commutes. The TRP includes employee benefits to promote mass transit use, carpooling, biking, or walking to reduce the number of miles traveled for employee commutes. The goal of the program is for all worksites to have no more than 60% of employees commuting via signal occupancy vehicle (SOV). In 2024, the City had 32 worksites with over 50 employees. Two worksites achieved an SOV rate below 60% and the average SOV rate of all sites was 76%.

column20: Increased temperatures manifested as heat waves and sustained high heat days directly harm human health through heat-related illnesses (mild heat stress to fatal heat stroke) and the exacerbation of pre-existing conditions in the medically fragile, chronically ill, and vulnerable. Lack of air conditioning increases risk of illness or death in extreme heat events, which pose the greatest risk to the elderly; people with mental illness, chronic conditions, or low incomes; people who are homeless or incarcerated; and those experiencing social or health-related vulnerabilities. Increased heat also intensifies the photochemical reactions that produce smog and ground level ozone and fine particulates (PM2.5), which contribute to and exacerbate respiratory disease in children and adults. Increased heat and carbon dioxide enhance the growth of plants that produce pollen, which are associated with allergies. Increased temperatures add to the heat load of buildings in urban areas and exacerbate existing urban heat islands adding to the risk of high ambient temperatures. In addition, violent crime has been shown to increase during heat events. All these impacts are likely to increase individuals' stress levels, potentially leading to mental health impacts.Drought, which is expected to occur more frequently with climate change, increases the risk of wildfires and reduces the amount of water available to fight wildfires. Climate change is also expected to cause fires to spread faster and burn more intensely in most vegetation types, particularly grassland. In addition to fire-related injuries, local and regional transport of smoke, ash, and fine particles increases respiratory and cardiovascular risks. Wildfires can also disrupt energy distribution, both directly by disrupting transmission lines and indirectly by causing utilities to shut down electricity distribution to avoid generating fire-starting sparks. Fire-associated power outages or shutdowns are life-threatening risks for residents who rely on electrically powered medical equipment such as respirators, and have already affected critical facilities including cooling centers, healthcare facilities, and assisted living facilities.Pandemics are expected to become more frequent as climate change continues to degrade natural habitats.

In the past two years, the Israeli Ministry of Health (MOH) has undertaken a comprehensive effort to prepare the healthcare system for climate change. The MOH's work has included mapping all relevant stakeholders, reviewing local and international literature, and consulting with representatives from the civil sector and government ministries. 
The Ministry of Health's action plan is built on several pillars:
Organizational Infrastructure and Staff Training: Developing a measurement and evaluation framework, training healthcare staff on climate change impacts, and appointing a dedicated official within the ministry to oversee climate change preparedness.
Green Healthcare System: Establishing a steering committee to define criteria for a 'green' healthcare system, pooling government resources to reduce emissions in health institutions, and setting incentives and regulations to promote green hospitals.
Emergency and Extreme Event Preparedness: Consolidating climate scenarios into a single, dedicated climate emergency plan for the healthcare system and conducting readiness drills to monitor preparedness levels.
Nutrition and Food Security: Promoting plant-based institutional food and sustainable food systems at the local level. Adaptation efforts include regulating nutritional enrichment to restore essential minerals lost due to climate change and ensuring access to healthy food for vulnerable populations.
Planning, Construction, and Environmental Conditions: Integrating climate and health considerations into urban planning and construction, maintaining the urban environment to prevent climate-related health hazards, and conducting health impact assessments for national projects with potential air pollution or other significant health risks.
Data and Research: Developing a dashboard to monitor infectious diseases and acute and chronic health conditions related to climate change. 
Public Awareness: Educating the public on the health consequences of climate change, both in routine and emergency situations.
The Municipality of Tel Aviv-Yafo acknowledges that climate change poses a direct threat to public health. While local authorities have a relatively limited impact on healthcare services, the city's strategy is to enhance collaboration with health maintenance organizations (HMOs) to better integrate climate adaptation measures into existing health frameworks.
The city's approach focuses on a multi-faceted plan that includes:
Public Awareness and Education: Developing educational campaigns to inform residents on how to manage their health during heatwaves and extreme heat events.
Infrastructure Adaptation: Expanding the network of public drinking water facilities and adapting recreational services to a warmer climate. This also includes preparing the city's beaches for heat, with the possibility of designating new beach areas for public use.

column20: Msunduzi is located in a hollow formed by the valleys of the uMsunduzi River and its tributaries. On clear winter nights, katabatic flow occurs, resulting in the movement of air from upslope areas down to the city bowl, much like water. This fills the valley floor with cold, dense air, creating an inversion that does not allow pollutants to escape. This air movement also brings pollutants from the entire Municipality into the valley, where it remains trapped by the inversion layer. The majority of industrial development within Msunduzi has been established within this inversion layer, as this land is both flat and in close proximity to both road and rail transport routes. As a result, the city suffers short-term peaks in pollution, despite relatively few heavy industries. Reported trends in air quality are as follows: • There has been a decreasing trend in smoke generation over the last 30 years. • Sporadic ambient monitoring of sulphur dioxide concentrations indicates decreases at two of the six sites while all the other monitoring sites show an increase. • An Increase of pollution within the Northdale-Willowton basin (Baynespruit Valley) has been noted. • High ambient benzene concentrations that exceed health standards were recorded. Benzene emissions are usually associated with vehicular emissions. • The presence of sulphurous compounds (sulphur dioxide and/or hydrogen sulphide) has been suggested as the cause of most of the public's odour complaints. Within Msunduzi, there are four main sources of air pollution: • An increase in vehicle volumes and traffic congestions in peak hours, particularly in the CBD and many of the arterial routes; • A large majority of industries operating old and dated technologies that have higher emissions than modern alternatives; • Formal and informal settlements that use coal and firewood for heating and cooking; and • Burning of sugar cane and brush wood.In order to effectively implement and control air quality, it is necessary to monitor and measure the concentrations of criteria pollutants in the ambient atmosphere. In terms of the AQA, it is mandatory for municipalities to monitor and report ambient air quality in compliance with Section 8 of the Act. Section 15(2) of the AQA requires each municipality to include an Air Quality Management Plan in its integrated development (IDP) plan required in terms of Chapter 5 of the Municipal Systems Act. An AQMP has been budgeted for in the 2017/2018 budget. In complying with its legislative mandate in terms of the NEM: AQA, the Environmental Health Sub-Unit operates a network of air quality monitoring stations located at City Hall, Oribi Airport, Edendale and Northdale (in partnership with KZN Department of Environmental Affairs).The pollutants that are monitored by the Msunduzi Air Quality Monitoring Network include Carbon monoxide (CO), Nitrogen oxides (NOx), ozone (O3), particulate matter of less than 2.5 microns (PM2.5) and 10 microns (PM10), Sulphur dioxide (SO2), and in future, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), in particular, a group of aromatic hydrocarbons, Benzene (C6H6), Toluene (C7H8), Ethyl-Benzene (C6H5CH2CH3) and Xylene (C8H10), referred to as the (BTEX) group. These are classified as criteria pollutants by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) and are the most commonly found air pollutants that can harm human health or the environment. In addition to the above, a range of meteorological parameters are also monitored i.e. wind speed, wind direction, rainfall, temperature, barometric pressure, relative humidity and solar radiation.

Um dos principais efeitos observados é o aumento súbito da demanda por atendimentos durante períodos de ondas de calor, enchentes e deslizamentos. Esses eventos geram sobrecarga em prontos-atendimentos, unidades de pronto atendimento (UPAs) e unidades básicas de saúde, elevando o número de internações por doenças respiratórias, cardiovasculares e infecciosas. Essa sobrecarga também compromete estoques de medicamentos e insumos hospitalares, dificultando o atendimento adequado à população.
Outro impacto importante ocorre na infraestrutura física das unidades de saúde. Inundações e alagamentos podem impedir o acesso de ambulâncias, dificultar o deslocamento de pacientes e danificar equipamentos sensíveis, como refrigeradores de vacinas e sistemas de suporte à vida. Além disso, quedas de energia e o rompimento de vias podem levar à interrupção dos serviços de saúde em momentos críticos. Em resposta, Salvador implementou, em 2024, o Plano Multirriscos de Saúde Pública, com protocolos de preparação e resposta em saúde para situações de emergência climática.
As mudanças climáticas também intensificam a ocorrência de surtos de doenças, exigindo maior esforço da vigilância epidemiológica. Chuvas intensas e elevação da temperatura favorecem a disseminação de doenças de veiculação hídrica, como leptospirose e hepatite A, além de arboviroses como dengue e chikungunya. O aumento desses surtos demanda mais capacidade laboratorial, atuação de equipes em campo e ações preventivas.
A sobrecarga dos profissionais de saúde também é um problema relevante. Situações de emergência climática exigem jornadas prolongadas, maior exposição ocupacional e atuação sob condições adversas, o que contribui para o estresse físico e emocional das equipes e compromete a continuidade da assistência. O PMAMC propõe a capacitação de profissionais para atuação em cenários de risco climático, com foco na mitigação dos impactos humanos e operacionais.

A sobrecarga das unidades de saúde durante eventos extremos (como ondas de calor, enchentes e deslizamentos) dificulta o atendimento rápido e eficaz, o que contribui para o agravamento de quadros clínicos. Isso se traduz em aumento nas taxas de morbidade e mortalidade evitáveis, especialmente entre crianças, idosos, pessoas com doenças crônicas e populações que vivem em áreas de risco.
As interrupções nos serviços de saúde, por danos estruturais ou falhas no fornecimento de energia elétrica, reduzem a capacidade de oferta de cuidados contínuos, como vacinação, tratamentos de doenças crônicas (diabetes, hipertensão, doenças respiratórias) e atendimento pré-natal. A ausência desses cuidados pode resultar em piores desfechos clínicos e hospitalares, com maior número de internações e complicações evitáveis.
O aumento da frequência e intensidade de doenças relacionadas ao clima, como arboviroses (dengue, zika, chikungunya), doenças hídricas (diarreias, hepatite A, leptospirose) e respiratórias (asma, bronquite, DPOC), afeta diretamente os indicadores de saúde pública. Esses agravos impactam especialmente regiões com menor infraestrutura urbana e saneamento. 
Além disso, o estresse contínuo dos profissionais de saúde e a precarização das condições de trabalho durante emergências climáticas comprometem a qualidade do atendimento e a segurança dos pacientes, afetando negativamente os indicadores de satisfação, eficiência do sistema e resolutividade clínica.
Estudos recentes da Fiocruz Bahia mostram, por exemplo, que a poluição atmosférica urbana, agravada por altas temperaturas e baixa arborização, está associada ao aumento de internações e mortes por doenças respiratórias em Salvador. A substituição da frota de ônibus por veículos menos poluentes poderia evitar dezenas de mortes por ano, indicando a relação direta entre políticas climáticas e melhora nos indicadores de mortalidade e expectativa de vida.
Por fim, o acúmulo de eventos extremos e doenças associadas ao clima também tem impactos na saúde mental da população, incluindo quadros de ansiedade, depressão e transtornos pós-traumáticos, especialmente entre pessoas que vivem em áreas atingidas por alagamentos e desastres. Isso amplia a demanda por serviços de saúde mental, que muitas vezes são insuficientes para atender à crescente complexidade dos casos.

column20: With the already-dangerous heat conditions in Florida, these significant increases in temperatures, in terms of individual days, averages, and seasonal changes, present serious implications for the health of local residents. The risk for heat-related health impacts is highest amongst infants, young children, the elderly over 65, those already ill, athletes, those spending time outside, including outdoor workers, those engaging in physical activity, and those who don't have access to air conditioning (Climate Central, “U.S. faces dramatic rise in extreme heat, humidity”, 2016), as well as those in more urban areas within the city, due an increase in the Urban Heat Island effect (Environmental Protection Agency & Center for Disease Control, 2016). Since 9.4% of Orlando's residents are over the age of 65, 7.1% are under five years old, and one-in-five of all residents (20.2%) live at or below the poverty line, which is above average among the lower 48 states (U.S. Census Bureau, 2017), we have a large representation of groups are considered to be especially vulnerable to extreme heat. Furthermore, during dangerously hot days, the risk for these heat-related effects sharply increases and can reach even healthy young adults to middle-aged individuals. According to current predictions, annual heat-related deaths will increase to tens-of-thousands by the end of the century (Climate Central, “U.S. faces dramatic rise in extreme heat, humidity”, 2016), and, with the projections for our region, many of these deaths will occur in Central Florida. For individuals and families with pets that spend some or all of their time outside or do not have air conditioning, this also presents a serious risk (Florida Division of Emergency Management, 2013). These heat impacts may also provide a strain on the healthcare system when faced with increased hospitalizations and doctors' visits, need for home care, and insurance claims. (Climate Central, “U.S. faces dramatic rise in extreme heat, humidity”, 2016). There is also an increasing frequency of dangerous heat days: “Florida currently has an average of 25 dangerous heat days each year. By 2050, it is projected to see 130 such days each year, more than any other state. The impacts from high heat also interact with other climate hazards that can result in amplified risks. This elevated heat can contribute to stagnant air, which has been increasing in Central Florida, and allows dangerous levels of both air pollutants and ground-level ozone to build up in the local area (Climate Central, “Stagnant air on the rise, upping ozone risk”, 2016). The consequences include respiratory issues and increased risk of air-borne disease. Extreme heat can also compound drought conditions, elevated sink hole risks, and increased algae blooms and bacteria present in water (Climate Central, “U.S. faces dramatic rise in extreme heat, humidity”, 2016). Increases in extreme heat can lead to elevated hospitalizations, illness and death with a large segment of the population at risk. This danger is further elevated as an occupational hazard for that work outside, such as construction workers, crossing guards, athletes, landscaping professionals, groundskeepers, etc. Today, 1 in 3 American households struggle to afford their energy bills, and 1 in 5 are forced to decide between energy and other necessities (EIA RECS 2015). In Orange County Florida, energy affordability threatens the 175,470 households living below 200% of the federal poverty level. Cumulatively, these homes experienced a HEAG of $263.5 million in 2017 alone (Home Energy Affordability Report, 2018). This equates to $1,501 per household in energy costs above the affordability threshold, roughly equal to the state average ($1,507). HEAG trends are severe in Florida, with a HEAG Index of 195.2 compared to the national average of 123.4. This reflects a doubling of the FL HEAG since the 2011 baseline. As extreme heat patterns intensify, these trends can be anticipated to increase and threaten low-income populations capacity to afford energy and other critical needs. Residents who do not have easy access to air-conditioning, cannot afford to cool their homes regularly, who have homes without proper weatherization, or those who need to walk, bike, or take public transportation are all at higher risk to extreme heat, even before health and age are factored in. Thus, low-income residents are at a disproportionately high risk for elevated heat events. We are reliant on grants to support energy equity work in these low-income communities that face the highest levels of energy burden. Funding can support energy upgrades, such as free efficient window AC units or portable batteries. We want to both reduce energy costs while improving quality of life for residents, with respect to heat.

column20: Droughts lead to water scarcity, negatively impacting agriculture and reducing food availability, which can lead to malnutrition, particularly among low-income households and rural farming communities. Vižmarje-Brod also provides accessible plots designed for people with mobility impairments (featuring raised beds, solid surfaces, and wider spacing). Community gardens harvest rainwater for irrigation, and mandatory composting promotes soil fertility while reducing organic waste. Assessments of climate change impacts on health outcomes and health services.
1. Health and wellbeing impacts of 2023 extreme weather events.
The extreme weather events of early 2023 (Cyclone Hale, the Auckland Anniversary heavy rainfall, and Cyclone Gabrielle) caused a lot of damage in communities across Tāmaki Makaurau. They were collectively the most severe and destructive weather events in New Zealand's recent history. They resulted in significant devastation to property and ongoing trauma for communities. Three researches have been undertaken to assess the impacts on health and wellbeing. They all identified significant impacts of the weather events on individuals and whānau physically, spiritually and emotionally. Identified needs were linked to a range of issues including ongoing trauma from the events, anxiety about future adverse weather events, stress in addressing the impacts of the events, isolation and loneliness, grief, unsuitable accommodation options and family and relationship stressors. Web link: https://www.knowledgeauckland.org.nz/media/ru2fjavn/research-summary-impacts-and-needs-of-aucklanders-2023-severe-weather-events-auckland-recovery-sep-2024.pdf
2. Daily heat stress sending children to hospital.
A study shows hospital admissions for children, for all sorts of ailments, rise when the temperature exceeds 24.1 degrees Celsius. This includes children in Auckland. Web link: https://www.auckland.ac.nz/en/news/2024/10/03/daily-heat-stress.html
3. Urban heat assessment 2024.
A geospatial heat dataset has been recently developed to provide detailed information of how temperatures vary across Auckland and the factors influencing these temperatures. It combines geospatial data, climate information and a physics-based urban heat model, accounting for multiple factors that influence urban heat island, such as land cover, building shape and size, heat emissions, and the urban climate. This initiative is part of Auckland Council's commitment to protecting the health and wellbeing of Auckland's communities today and into the future. By understanding and addressing the urban heat island effect, the council and its partners are working to ensure all Aucklanders can thrive in a warmer region. The report provides the information needed to understand the impacts of heat on Auckland's vulnerable communities. Work is already underway to address the city's heat pockets. Web link: https://www.knowledgeauckland.org.nz/media/goliai5f/auckland-urban-heat-assessment-technical-report-arup-oct-2024.pdf

The report assessed the impact of climate change on health, in particular to heat risks (heat vulnerability). Web link: https://www.knowledgeauckland.org.nz/media/tvzhmmtt/tr2019-019-climate-change-risks-in-auckland-arup-march-2019-final.pdf
5. Health National Adaptation Plan 2024 - 2027.
This first Health National Adaptation Plan (HNAP) is an important step towards placing health considerations at the forefront of the climate response of Aotearoa New Zealand (New Zealand). It sets the strategic direction and provides national-level priority actions for health-focused adaptation to climate change. The HNAP sets the foundation for the regional or local climate health action plans (CHAPs) that Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora (Health NZ), including the National Public Health Service, will develop. Web link: https://www.health.govt.nz/system/files/2024-10/Health%20National%20Adaptation%20Plan%202024-2027_0.pdf

There is also a need to assess and address health equity issues due to disparities in gender and income between regions. Goyang City has set the vision of 'a smart health city of Goyang that realizes a healthy and balanced life' for the 8th Local Healthcare Plan. To systematically achieve this vision, four strategic directions, thirteen initiatives, and thirty-seven detailed tasks have been selected for implementation.
The four main strategies are: addressing health disparities through strategies to eliminate blind spots, smart health management based on information and communication technology, creating a health environment based on multi-sectoral cooperation within the region, and strengthening community infection response and health safety networks.

Accessibility to health care infrastructure is essential to improve living standards and reduce vulnerability to climate and other disasters. Slum dwellers and people with special needs, with limited access to emergency service infrastructure, public transport, and green spaces, are more vulnerable to extreme climate events.

Accessibility to health care services has been examined spatially, in line with the Urban and Regional Development Plan Formulation and Implementation (URDPFI) guidelines and the Development Plan of Ahmedabad.

Hospitals are marked spatially and correlated with urban flood risk areas to identify critical areas with limited accessibility due to water logging/ urban flood. 651 out of 2,080 hospitals are affected due to urban flood. In areas such as Maninagar, at least 19 hospitals are affected.

Ahmedabad has 2,080 hospitals with a capacity of 34,432 beds (5 beds per 1000 persons), exceeding the WHO guideline of 3 beds per 100 persons. Around 99.7% of the population (7.2 million people) has easy access (within 3km distance) to health care facilities. Considering the cost of treatment in private hospitals, accessibility to government health care facilities (including Community Health Centres of AMC), especially for slum dwellers, has been examined separately. Residents of slums in Vatva, Shyamal and Dudeshwar areas need to travel more than 4.5 km to access government hospitals. Slums in these areas are at high risk due to exposure to extreme heat and urban flood risks and limited accessibility to government health care facilities.

Population rendered vulnerable due to distant health care facilities: 0.25% of the total population in the city (18,000 people); 20% of all slum dwellers (0.2 million slum population).

Further details on accessibility to health care facilities: 94.1% of the total population (6.7 million people) can access health care facilities within 1 km, 4.7% (0.3 million people) within 2 km, and 1% (75,000 people) within 3 km. 25% of all slum dwellers (0.2 million people) can access health care facilities within 1 km, 27% within 2 km, and 27% within 3 km.

Refer section 4.3.5.5 (page no. 146) of Ahmedabad Climate Resilient City Action Plan - Towards A Net Zero Future 2070

column20: One of the main concerns of public health systems is heat waves, whose effects are more pronounced in urban areas. The main causes of hospital admission, resulting from excessive heat, are related to cardiovascular problems, changes in blood pressure and lack of cerebral oxygenation, breathing difficulties and kidney and liver failure. There are still few quantitative studies that analyse the effects of the urban heat island on human health in Portugal (Almeida et al. 2010). Data from 2000 to 2018 suggests that heat waves in Portugal caused daily hospital admissions to increase by 18,9%. Like extreme heat, extreme cold can increase the pressure on health system, with the increase in infections of respiratory or lung diseases, also due to very old and inefficient housing. The need to heat homes also contributed to the increase in hospitalizations, either due to the impacts of the cold or due to smoke or gas inhalation, with the increased use of fireplaces or other similar heating systems.

Extreme heat causes more deaths than any other climate-related hazard. People in areas with less tree canopy coverage and less access to air conditioning are highly vulnerable to increasing extreme heat and heat waves. Lower income neighborhoods and communities of color often have fewer trees, putting these communities at higher risk. Elderly people are very sensitive to heat, as are infants and people with existing health conditions. Higher temperatures can also increase the formation of ground-level ozone, a key component of smog. Ground level ozone causes many health impacts, including increased incidence of asthma and increased incidence of premature death from heart and lung disease.

Severe thunderstorms are a major source of catastrophic loss. Severe storms can cause energy outages and flooding. During energy outages, some of the most vulnerable populations include medically-sensitive populations and elders, because the loss of power can lead to exposure to extreme heat or cold, as well as failure of vital medical equipment. Flood waters often become contaminated with hazardous materials that can impact human health and contaminate drinking water. People most vulnerable to flood impacts include those living in high flood risk areas, and especially those with limited mobility, such as elders, homeless, and people without vehicles.

With warmer and wetter winters, diseases such as mosquito-borne West Nile Virus, dengue, and Zika, as well as tick-borne Lyme disease, and Ehrlichiosis, could become more prevalent. Water-borne diseases, such as cryptosporidium, are strongly linked with increasing rainfall extremes such as those experienced in the region in recent years.

A primary climate change vulnerability identified for Louisville Metro's residents is the potential for an over-burdened healthcare industry tasked with responding to multiple or increasing threats of outbreaks and extreme events. State and local health agencies and vector control organizations are responsible for detecting and responding to diseases. Increasing capacity will be needed for continued tracking, diagnosing, and reporting of cases of known and new illnesses.

This report provided the assessment of the risk and vulnerability of the City of Tshwane's residents to health impacts from heat for the current climate. This assessment provided a baseline assessment, which will be compared with future projections of climate change. This assessment used high-resolution exposure and vulnerability indicators to provide a spatially detailed risk assessment for the City. The exposure assessment considered two variables in order to unravel the potential risk to health from exposure to heat, namely, i) high maximum temperatures and ii) high minimum temperatures. These have a different spatial distribution in Tshwane, as they do in many cities due to the impact of UHI, and thus both needed to be considered when working to understand the risk to human health. The Vulnerability Assessment was comprised of three vulnerability indices that speak to the vulnerability of households (socio-economic vulnerability), the vulnerability of the infrastructure that supports them (settlement fabric vulnerability), and the vulnerability of the environment that supports these activities (environmental vulnerability). Vulnerability is thus the propensity or predisposition to be adversely affected by a hazard and is present within communities before they encounter a hazard. Socio-economic vulnerability (SEV) is a composite indicator that speaks to the vulnerability of households within a community. It is a composite indicator that addresses four indicators and seven variables including household composition (household size, age dependency), income composition (unemployment), education (literacy rates and level of education), and health (child mortality and comorbidities). A high vulnerability score indicates spatial areas with a high number of vulnerable households with regards to their ability to withstand adverse shocks from the external environment. The Socio-Economic Vulnerability Index shows that vulnerable pockets are distributed over all regions but is most notable in the following areas:•In the north-western part of Region 1•In the northern parts of Region 2•In the north to the centre of Region 3 and at its border with Region 4. •In the centre of Region 4, •where the northern border of Region 6 coincides with the southern border of Region 5. After combining the SEV with the population size in of each area, areas with the highest SEV are focused in the following areas:•In the central part of Region 1•At the border between Region 3 and 4 •In the southern part of Region 4, with the hot spot in the centre of Region 4 remaining. •In the northern part of Region 6 as well as •a few isolated areas in the north-west of Region 7.The aggregated effect of consecutive hot days and warm nights represents the worst exposure scenario to heat. The western and northern part of the CoT have the highest exposure to the combined effect of non-optimal temperatures. The following areas are thus considered risk hotspots for health impacts due to heat exposure and vulnerability before considering the effect of population size:•Regions 1 and 2 •Scattered areas in Region 5 and the northern parts of Region 3 and Region 6. When the population size of each hexagon is considered, heat-health risk hot spots are especially prevalent in the following areas:•Region 1 •the northern parts of Region 2 and Region 6 •with some isolated hot spots in Region 3, 4 and 7.

column20: Climate change directly influences on individuals' well-being and health, but this often happens through long-term, complex, and often concealed processes, including broader trends of urban development. Although a sudden hazard - such as a heat wave - may increase instantaneous mortality and morbidity, the casualties may represent the tip of the iceberg of those adversely affected by climate change, and the underlying processes. Urban populations, especially in socially and economically disadvantaged areas, are likely to be particularly vulnerable to the unfavorable effects of climate change, due to already existing exposure to e.g. air pollutants, social stressors and the urban heat island effect and a higher burden of major chronic conditions. These populations are also likely to reside in areas with less urban green space and be less able to take adaptive actions, further increasing their vulnerability to heat effects and other weather-related stresses. City of Turku is collaborating with universities on a long-term basis to improve our understanding of the interaction between urban environment, climate, human health and adaptation, and how such phenomena transform spatially and temporally. In these studies, novel integration and analysis of longitudinal cohort data, socio-economic and policy data, environmental land cover data, and fine-resolution climate scenarios are utilized. Through the collaboration we will gain actionable knowledge to integrate climate-health risks in our strategic planning.During 2018 when the Turku Climate Plan 2029 was first drafted, extensive studies on health-risks and vulnerability did not exist on national or local level. However, the situation has since improved. A national assessment on Weather and Climate Risks in Finland covering also health related risks and vulnerabilities was carried out in September 2018. The report contains an assessment of hydro-meteorological and climatic risks for different sectors in Finland. In addition, the Climate Change and Health Academy Programme (CLIHE) is investigating the impacts of climate change on human health and well-being in order to enhance the knowledge base for designing appropriate adaptation responses. CLIHE runs from 2020 to 2023 and comprises seven research consortium projects and three international joint research projects. Out of the seven projects Hercules-project (https://sites.utu.fi/hercules/) examines past and possible future changes in pattern and intensity of climate-related health risks in six cities: Helsinki, Espoo, Tampere, Vantaa, Turku & Oulu, to develop a dynamic pathways model of different policy outcomes, and to catalyze chances for improved evidence-based decision making.

As a result of climate change, the distribution areas of many plant species found in Finland may gradually shift further north. If there are changes in the distribution and flowering periods of allergenic plants, such as birch, this could be reflected in temporal changes in allergy symptoms at the population level. Warming temperatures could trigger the pollen season earlier than before if the growing season starts earlier in spring, as expected. Warming may also facilitate the spread of new allergenic species to Finland, and a longer growing season could extend the pollen season across the country. However, these changes are occurring slowly, and no increase in allergy cases has been demonstrated so far.

Warming temperatures, along with increased winter precipitation and flooding, may also affect the occurrence of allergies caused by molds, yeasts, and toxic algae, leading to an increase in allergies and respiratory diseases related to these organisms. Mild and rainy winters could further increase moisture damage in buildings, unless the changing climate is adequately considered in new construction and renovations.

En los años 2023 y 2024 se realizaron alrededor de 80 actuaciones, con la colocación y monitoreo de sensores de oviposición para la observación del control focal, y se desarrollaron actividades de capacitación a las organizaciones comunitarias y charlas informativas acerca de esta problemática. El cambio climático está teniendo un impacto profundo en la salud de la población de Rosario, exacerbando los desafíos que enfrentan los sistemas de salud locales. Los eventos climáticos extremos, como las olas de calor, las precipitaciones torrenciales y el aumento sostenido de las temperaturas medias, generan una serie de efectos adversos sobre la salud pública, que sobrecargan la capacidad del sistema de salud de la ciudad.

Uno de los impactos más críticos es el aumento de las enfermedades respiratorias y cardiovasculares, derivado del estrés térmico causado por el aumento de las temperaturas extremas. La población más vulnerable, incluidos los adultos mayores, los niños pequeños y las personas con enfermedades preexistentes, corre un mayor riesgo durante estos eventos. Según el informe de Mapas de Riesgo Climático de Rosario, se estima que más del 30% de la población de la ciudad se encuentra expuesta a riesgos graves durante olas de calor, lo que incrementa las hospitalizaciones y la demanda de atención médica.

Otro desafío significativo está relacionado con las precipitaciones torrenciales, que no solo provocan inundaciones sino que también aumentan la proliferación de enfermedades transmitidas por vectores, como el dengue y la leptospirosis. La acumulación de agua en áreas urbanas y la proliferación de basurales generan condiciones óptimas para la propagación de estos vectores. Como resultado, el riesgo de enfermedades vectoriales se ha incrementado en más del 27% en ciertas áreas de la ciudad.

Además, la interrupción de servicios esenciales como el suministro de agua potable y energía eléctrica durante estos eventos extremos afecta de manera directa la capacidad de los hospitales y centros de salud para brindar atención. La falta de acceso a agua potable y las fallas en los sistemas eléctricos pueden agravar las condiciones de salud de los pacientes y dificultar la operación eficiente de los centros de atención.

El sistema de salud de Rosario debe, por lo tanto, prepararse para una mayor presión, con una población cada vez más vulnerable a las enfermedades relacionadas con el clima, desde el estrés térmico hasta las infecciones vectoriales. La información contenida en los Mapas de Riesgo Climático resalta la importancia de un enfoque preventivo, fortaleciendo las infraestructuras críticas de salud para mitigar los efectos de los fenómenos climáticos extremos y asegurar la resiliencia de los servicios de salud en la ciudad.

Para más detalles sobre las áreas de mayor riesgo en Rosario, puede consultar los mapas en: https://www.rosario.gob.ar/inicio/mapas-de-riesgo-climatico-rosario-2024.

Para o enfrentamento de doenças relacionadas direta ou indiretamente às mudanças climáticas o município faz monitoramento emitindo alertas e informe semanais. Os alertas epidemiológicos são emitidos para divulgação de informações sobre a ocorrência de eventos com potencial risco à saúde, que incluem medidas necessárias à redução ou eliminação do risco. Esse documento informa as áreas responsáveis e profissionais como atuar nesses momentos específicos relacionados à diversas temáticas, como arbovirores e extremos climáticos. Em setembro de 2023 o Centro de Informações Estratégicas em Vigilância em Saúde (CIEVS-CG) emitiu um alerta referente a forte onda de calor no município que poderia infringir risco à saúde e à vida, especialmente de pessoas enfermas, idosas e crianças.
Especificamente relacionado às arboviroses são divulgados dados mensais da situação epidemiológica e de Infestação do Aedes aegypti (LIRAA) no site da Secretaria Municipal de Saúde, 
https://www.campogrande.ms.gov.br/sesau/downloads/

column20: Como modelo de cidade vulnerável a impactos climáticos, Teresina vem sentindo os efeitos das mudanças climáticas. De acordo com o Relatório de Vulnerabilidade Climática do Piauí, publicado em 2019, Teresina apresenta riscos decorrentes de secas prolongadas, enchentes, deslizamentos de terra e aumento da temperatura, que afetam a qualidade de vida da população e a economia local. A cidade já sofreu com eventos climáticos extremos, como as enchentes ocorridas em 2019, na Zona Sul de Teresina, que afetou em torno de 40 casas, deixou 30 pessoas feridas, ocasionou perdas materiais e humanas (G1, 2019). Em 2022, as chuvas que atingiram, principalmente a Zona Norte da cidade, desabrigaram 230 famílias, além de resultar em prejuízos para outras famílias e para o comércio local (G1, 2022). Em uma perspectiva de longo prazo, a Prefeitura de Teresina, alinhada aos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS) propostos pela ONU, vem encaminhando ações para a construção de um desenvolvimento municipal mais sustentável para a cidade por intermédio da Agenda 2030, uma pactuação entre poder público e sociedade para alcance das metas locais de desenvolvimento sustentável (PREFEITURA MUNICIPAL DE TERESINA, 2018). Parte dessas ações converge com a criação do Plano de Ação Climática.

À medida que o período de estiagem avança, Teresina enfrenta um cenário desafiador, com a combinação de altas temperaturas e a supressão vegetal. Essa época, caracterizada pelo clima seco, potencializa um dos maiores problemas da cidade: as queimadas. Elas não só destroem a vegetação local, mas também comprometem a qualidade do ar, tornando a respiração difícil para a população, especialmente para aqueles com problemas respiratórios crônicos.

Esse contexto de seca e calor acarreta consequências diretas para a vida na cidade. A demanda por água aumenta exponencialmente, pressionando a infraestrutura de abastecimento. Para as comunidades periféricas, que muitas vezes já lidam com acesso precário, a situação se agrava, expondo-as a uma maior vulnerabilidade social e sanitária. A escassez de água e a poluição do ar geram um aumento de problemas de saúde, como desidratação, infecções respiratórias e problemas dermatológicos, sobrecarregando o sistema de saúde público.

Apesar dos impactos negativos, o período de estiagem também é aproveitado para a realização de certas obras. É a época em que se torna possível a implantação de vazantes nas margens dos rios e em áreas próximas às rodovias.

column20: Eventos climáticos fora do setor de saúde têm repercussões significativas na população de João Pessoa. O calor extremo pressiona o setor energético, aumentando riscos de interrupções que afetam hospitais e serviços essenciais. O transbordamento de rios e inundações costeiras impacta transporte, habitação e saneamento, ampliando a exposição da população a doenças transmitidas pela água. A estiagem compromete o abastecimento hídrico e a produção agrícola, refletindo em insegurança alimentar e nutricional. Além disso, as doenças infecciosas estão diretamente relacionadas a fatores ambientais externos, como drenagem deficiente e gestão inadequada de resíduos. A Secretaria Municipal de Saúde reconhece esses impactos indiretos e, no âmbito do Plano Municipal de Saúde 2026-2029, encontra-se em fase de planejamento para integrar dados climáticos aos sistemas de vigilância epidemiológica e projetar cenários futuros, fortalecendo a capacidade de resposta às mudanças climáticas.

column20: Albuquerque's Water Utility Authority Water Conservation Plan sets a usage goal of 110 gallons per capita per day (GPCD) by 2037. The current GPCD is 121, so a reduction of about 1 gallon per person per day each year is all we need to reach that goal. This plan aligns with the utility's long-term water resources management strategy, WATER 2120, in which conservation plays a critical role as we face the uncertainties of climate change and population growth. To achieve the new conservation goal, the Water Authority will emphasize outdoor water savings. Conservation efforts will focus on providing tools for improving irrigation efficiency while maintaining healthy and aesthetically pleasing xeric landscapes. The Water Authority offers a variety of educational and incentive programs to help increase water conservation throughout Albuquerque including rebates on water efficient appliances, rebates for xeriscaping efforts, workshops and events, and multiple guides and tips on water conservation. https://www.abcwua.org/Conservation_and_Rebates.aspx

column20: Henderson is vulnerable to climate change and the increased risk of extreme heat and drought. These hazards pose a health risk to residents and visitors to the City. The lack of resources and the steady growth of the population increases the health risks to a larger population than before. Extreme heat periods pose risks including heat exhaustion, heatstroke, dehydration and can worsen pre-existing health conditions. Vulnerable populations such as low-income seniors and individuals experiencing homelessness are more susceptible to heat related illnesses and death from extreme heat periods. In 2024, the Southern Nevada Health District reported 90 heat-related hospitalizations at Henderson Hospital. Henderson's other hospitals do not currently report heat related hospitalizations. Drought can lead to decrease in our consumptive water supply and pose health risks to the growing population. In extreme cases of drought, infectious diseases from water scarcity and reduced food availability can impact larger populations while also worsening air quality. Vulnerable populations have limited access to resources and health services and may be more affected by malnutrition and water-borne diseases. Droughts can negatively affect air quality and can lead to an increase in dust storms and wildfires, due to the limited amount of water available.

column20: Higher daytime temperatures and more days with high dew points have resulted in more extreme heat events. An extreme heat event (EHE) is characterized by an abnormally high heat index, which takes into account air temperature and dew point temperature (MDH, 2014a & Seeley, 2015). Without precautions, extreme heat can cause heat-related illnesses characterized by heat rash, edema, breathing difficulties, muscle cramps, dizziness or fainting, profuse sweating, weakness, nausea or vomiting, dehydration, headache, confusion, unconsciousness, and even death. Extreme heat can also exacerbate existing illnesses and chronic health conditions (MDH, 2014a). June of 2021 was the second hottest on record. On June 20, 2022, the temperature reached 101 degrees, a new record for the day.

column20: Flash floods can trigger a plethora of direct and indirect human health effects. Flash flooding directly poses significant acute health threats, including drowning, injury, electrocution, and exposure to hazardous chemicals and sewage. Chronic health threats during the recovery phase of a flash flood include exposure to mold and mildew which may exacerbate respiratory illnesses. Individuals may be exposed to waterborne diseases, such as Cryptosporidium, E. coli O157, Legionella, and norovirus. Furthermore, exposure to and proper disposal of water-damaged debris, especially chemical waste, can pose additional health risks. Finally, mental stress can also be a direct health threat following a flash flood (MDH, 2015a).There are also several indirect health effects of flash flooding. Mental and physical stress may be triggered by economic loss due to flood damage, strained essential services, or high health care bills due to injury (MDH, 2015a). Business closures and lay-offs can also instigate stress and economic loss (MDH, 2014a). Disruptions in social and economic services as well as damaged infrastructure, such as roads, railways, water systems, and sewer systems may affect health. Finally, compromised food and water quality and supply can also affect human health. The resultant direct and indirect health effects are numerous after a flash flood and should be acknowledged in the context of planning emergency services to those most vulnerable and affected by this climate hazard. Several populations are vulnerable to flooding. According to MDH, these populations include the following: Older adults, especially living alone; those with physical or mental illnesses that hinder the ability for self-care; those under economic strain; those living in substandard housing or mobile homes; those without vehicle access; those with limited English proficiency; those who rely on private wells; and those with respiratory illnesses who may be susceptible to mold following flooding (MDH, 2014a).

column20: Since 2017, the percentage of mosquito pools that tested positive for WNV has increased in Windsor-Essex. During the surveillance period spanning from May to October of 2018, 26 (2.7%) positive pools of WNV were detected in mosquito traps, which is almost double the percentage of pools that tested positive in 2013. Furthermore, exotic species, such as Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus which are vectors of Zika virus have been discovered in the region since 2016. In 2021, there were 17 positive (0.7% of all pools) West Nile Virus Pools in Windsor/Essex County. And fortunately, no positive pools for Zika or Eastern Equine Encephalitis. \n\nSouthwestern Ontario is an established area for Lyme disease. There were 18 cases of Lyme disease in WEC between 2016 and 2018. Lyme disease active surveillance performed in the Fall 2018, identified black legged ticks. This recent finding was alarming since in the previous 3 years (2015-2017), no black legged ticks were captured and no ticks in general were captured after the month of May. Lone star ticks, whose bite can lead to alpha-gal meat allergy, were also found during active surveillance in 2017. These have also been found consistently in the region through public tick submissions from 2015 to 2018. In 2024, there were 17 cases of Lyme disease that were reported, being the highest number in the last decade (https://windsornewstoday.ca/windsor/news/2025/06/03/windsor-essex-sees-record-number-of-lyme-disease-cases-in-2024).

column20: Wild fires in the south of Spain are a potential risk to the health of the public in Gibraltar. There have currently been no impacts from these fires as the likelihood of impact is highly reliant on prevailing wind patters. If a fire occurs near the border in southern Spain and the wind direction favours Gibraltar, there would be impact from fire smoke causing air-pollution related illness. However, due to the small size of Gibraltar and its exposure to coastal weather, it is likely the smoke would continue to move off the coast quickly and would not stagnate in populated areas. Wild fires in the south of Spain are also a potential risk to health service provision in Gibraltar. Approximately 50% of the nursing staff in Gibraltar travel across the frontier every day to work. If a fire occurs near the border in southern Spain, this could prevent nursing/hospital staff from reaching the hospital. In this case, the hospital may become overwhelmed due to staff shortages. This is considered a vulnerability by the hospital.

No âmbito da elaboração da EMAAC de Matosinhos foi realizado um levantamento das vulnerabilidades climáticas locais, para perceber como os efeitos adversos afetaram as atividades, as pessoas e as infraestruturas do concelho. Os danos para a saúde (doença, ferimentos, morte, etc) foram identificados como exemplo(s) de impactos decorrentes dos riscos climáticos.
Particularmente no caso de episódios de temperaturas baixas/ondas de frio há danos registados a nível da saúde, nomeadamente havendo necessidade de transporte de sem-abrigos e de animais para prevenir os seus impactes.
Os eventos mais extremos têm consequências na saúde e impactam o aumento da mortalidade na população mais vulnerável. 
As ondas de frio e calor são também particularmente impactantes e/ou tem efeitos mais exacerbados para as populações em condições de pobreza energética. 
Não existem ainda estudos específicos que permitam ao município saber com exatidão efeitos das alterações climáticas na saúde da sua população (i.e: Nº de pessoas afetadas por doenças derivadas das alterações climáticas). Contudo, sabe-se que Portugal está sujeito ao aumento da mortalidade causada por vagas de calor e a transmissão de doenças através de insetos ( https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/pt/headlines/society/20180905STO11945/os-efeitos-das-alteracoes-climaticas-na-europa-infografia). 
Anualmente morrem cerca de 200 pessoas em Portugal devido aos efeitos das alterações climáticas (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(06)68901-0/fulltext#back-bib5). 
Existem diferentes estudos à escala nacional ou com enfoque em determinados grupos de doentes que relacionam as alterações climáticas e os fenómenos mais extremos com os impactos na saúde. 
Doenças respiratórias como asma ou bronquite, insolações, doenças de pele, fadiga, problemas renais e cardíacos são frequentemente associados ao aumento da temperatura e da poluição, que pode ainda ter efeitos negativos na gravidez. 
O calor excessivo também torna mais difícil o trabalho e o exercício físico, além de prejudicar o sono, com efeito no descanso e na recuperação do corpo. 
Os fenómenos extremos levam também a mortes prematuras - quer de idosos quer de pessoas que sofram de doenças.

The City of Tempe is experiencing rapid growth, leading to an increase in impervious surfaces, while rising carbon emissions are further intensifying the urban heat island effect. ocal climate records show that over the past 50 years, temperatures in the Phoenix area have risen by nearly 3.6°F. This warming trend poses serious concerns for economic stability, quality of life, and public health. Extreme heat is the most prevalent hazard in Maricopa County, where Tempe is located, and it causes more deaths than all other natural hazards combined.

High temperatures alone are not the sole drivers of heat-related illness and death—social factors also play a critical role in a person's ability to cope. Populations most vulnerable to extreme heat include people over the age of 65, individuals living alone or below the poverty line, the unhoused, and outdoor workers. As temperatures rise, health systems will face growing demand and strain, stretching their capacity, staff, and resources.

In addition, climate change places increasing pressure on the agricultural sector through prolonged heat and drought, making it harder to grow local food and ensure access to healthy, affordable options for the community.

This will have a public health impact for populations sensitive and vulnerable to extreme heat. While extreme heat is not as common in Flagstaff as in southern Arizona, there are cases of heat-related illness and death. From 2005-2015, there were 18 deaths in Coconino County from exposure to excessive natural heat, and approximately 20 emergency department visits and hospital inpatient stays. Data are not available on how many of these cases occurred in Flagstaff or were treated there. However, as the largest city in the county, Flagstaff's public health services may be called on more in the future to treat cases of extreme heat. By 2100, 30 to 80 days per year are expected to be above 90°F, compared to just 2 days per year between 1950 and 2017. This projected increase in days above 90°F could increase the risk of heat-related illness and death, especially for those who work outdoors, those who are experiencing homelessness, and households currently without air conditioning. Low-income households already struggling to afford basic needs could be particularly vulnerable to extreme heat without affordable options for air conditioning or refuge from extreme heat. The risk is further increased for emergency workers and first responders tasked with responding to summer wildfires. Hotter summers in southern Arizona and fewer snow-based recreation opportunities locally may shift some of Flagstaff's recreation and tourism to the summer months and shoulder seasons (spring and fall). National economic studies suggest gains in warm-season tourism may compensate for losses in cold-season tourism. However, Flagstaff's already-robust tourism infrastructure may need additional capacity to meet higher demand. With visitors concentrated in the warm season, unintended environmental stresses such as greater water demand or increased trampling of natural areas may also occur. Despite City efforts, housing costs are expected to continue to rise in Flagstaff as the population grows, Baby Boomers retire, and purchases of second homes increase. As temperatures increase in southern Arizona, and visitation or second homes to Flagstaff increase, housing pressures in Flagstaff may worsen. High-severity wildfires have already had negative impacts on parts of the broader Flagstaff region, causing severe flooding, loss of recreational opportunities, and even loss of life. The longer and more severe wildfire season has increased resource demands on City firefighting staff. In the future, high-severity wildfires could have serious implications: - immediate threats to public health from an active wildfire, including threats to health from fire, smoke, and evacuations. - a mass evacuation would have negative implications for the local community. In the event of an evacuation, those without homes, adequate transport, or with limited disposable income are at greater risk of negative consequences. Longer-term effects include economic losses for local businesses, loss of income for residents, and mental health effects. - More frequent, high-severity wildfires will also pose threats to buildings and infrastructure, potentially impairing the ability to render services to residents in the short and long term. - After fires, local watershed health may be greatly impacted, with long-term water quality impacts for both the natural environment and drinking water systems. - Post-wildfire flooding is an enormous and highly consequential threat, with the risk of losing lives, and a large portion of Flagstaff's downtown and the NAU campus are at risk of flooding if certain areas were to burn in a high-severity wildfire. - Even if the wildfire does not pose an immediate threat to Flagstaff residents, visitors and infrastructure, an increase in wildfires likely will increase demand on the City resources, to respond to wildfire events. Wildfires will cause increases in respiratory and other illnesses related to prevalence of smoke-filled air adversely affects community health.

Additionally, wildfire risk will also be influenced by potential changes in vegetation. This lethal hazard has already been experienced on an alarming scale in neighboring communities and cities in California. California has also been hit by extreme heat and lightning storms that have ignited massive wildfires. In 2020 alone, 4.4 million acres were burned in CA wildfires, making air quality horrific throughout much of the State for months at a time. With both the extreme heat events and wildfire risk, we have experienced rolling power outages over the past few years as the utility has struggled to meet cooling demands as well as has engaged in preventative \'Public Safety Power Shutdowns\' to reduce the risk of additional fire outbreak caused by sparking power lines.

column20: Fremont can experience extreme heat days, where the Heat Index, a function of heat and relative humidity, is high. Extreme heat days pose a public health threat, causing symptoms, such as, exhaustion, heat cramps, and sunstroke if the Heat Index is over 90 F. Heat emergencies occur when residents are subject to heat exhaustion and heatstroke and are more likely to occur in areas not adapted to heat and without air conditioning, cooling centers, or vegetation to mediate heat impacts in exposed areas. Certain populations are typically the most at risk during extreme heat emergencies, including people with disabilities, chronic diseases, the elderly, and children. Climate change is expected to generate an increase in ambient average air temperature, particularly in the summer. The frequency, intensity, and duration of extreme heat events and heat waves are also expected as regional climate impacts. The increase of extreme hot days will negatively impact our residents, especially our elderly residents and other vulnerable populations. Direct impacts of extreme heat include increases in heat-related illnesses such as heat-stroke, dehydration, and heat-related mortality such as heart disease. High temperatures can also exacerbate the impact of pre-existing conditions such as diabetes and renal disease. Higher temperatures and stagnant air also worsen Fremont's air quality and lead to higher rates of respiratory illness, asthma, and allergies. Indirect impacts of extreme heat include exacerbating behavioral health problems. . Higher temperatures and increased duration of these high-temperature days will also lead to higher energy demands to cool homes and buildings, which will strain our resources and result in the use of highly polluting peaker plants to meet energy demands.

The recently completed 2020 Qualitative Climate Risk Assessment for Quezon City has identified key climate risks from (a) drought, (b) heat and (c) cyclones and flooding that will specifically impact low-income and vulnerable groups and communities such as children, youth, informal settler communities, and the elderly population.

1. Prioritized impacts from heat with significant impact on key vulnerable sectors:- Heat stress causing illness & loss of life (also to livestock): Extreme heat conditions cause related diseases and can cause even death. Vulnerable groups include elderly and outside construction workers.- Increase of water- and vector-borne diseases: Increased temperatures are linked with the increased transmission of vector and waterborne diseases like dengue and polio- Increasing water shortages: During heat waves, water use is increasing, impacting especially vulnerable poor groups.

2. Prioritized impacts from drought with significant impact on key vulnerable sectors:- Decrease in (dam) water availability: Long dry spells have caused problems in water availability as dams get depleted. Service interruptions and water rationing measures might be needed more often, impacting poor communities more.- Increase of drought-related health impacts: Particulate matter suspended in the air can irritate lungs, causing chronic respiratory illnesses.- Threatened food security: Damages to crops and drops in yield will be felt the most by poor communities

3. Prioritized impacts from flooding with significant impact on key vulnerable sectors:- Displacement and loss of lives because of storms and floods:nd injuries like contusions, fractures and electrocution- Post-flood disease outbreaks: Extreme rainfall and the resulting floods may lead to increased transmission of infectious diseases. Systematic failures of healthcare systems could lead to increased fatalities.- Threatened access to safe drinking water after flooding: After floods many people in Quezon City do not have access to safe drinking water, especially the urban poor.- Threatened food security: Excessive rainfall and strong typhoons could inflict serious damages to agricultural crops. After extreme rainfall, access to food can be limited which could also influence the general condition of the population, including malnutrition and the lack of adequate immunity.

Climate change impacts on health outcomes and health services in Helsingborg

Helsingborg's Quality of Life Programme highlights several important links between climate, environment, and health. The city is working to reduce climate impact and strengthen resilience through instruments such as the Climate and Energy Plan, the Climate Adaptation Plan, and the Stormwater Plan. The programme underlines that air pollution, noise, and limited access to green areas negatively affect health, while access to nature and opportunities for recreation contribute to improved physical and mental well-being. It also draws attention to challenges such as mental health issues, social isolation, and unequal exposure to environmental risks across different neighbourhoods.

However, the programme does not provide a detailed analysis of direct climate-related health impacts, such as heatwaves, vector-borne diseases, or the effects of extreme weather events on vulnerable groups. Nor does it address in detail how health and care services may be strained by climate change or specify quantitative indicators to monitor these impacts. Further work is therefore needed to assess direct health outcomes of climate change and to develop adaptation strategies within the healthcare sector.

column20: A local Heatwave Plan, including alert systems and details of the response coordination is updated yearly by the Public Health team in Brighton and Hove City Council. 2022 was the warmest year on record with temperatures in excess of 40 degrees recorded for the first time Climate and health security(https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/heat-mortality-monitoring-reports/heat-mortality-monitoring-report-2023). During four periods of heat in 2024, there were 1,311 heat-associated deaths in England. This was 282 more deaths than predicted, based on the observed temperatures and historic temperature-mortality trends. (https://ukhsa.blog.gov.uk/2025/06/11/heat-health-what-you-need-to-know-for-summer-2025/). A range of mild to severe health impacts can result from exposure to high temperatures including: • Headache, dizziness and confusion; loss of appetite and feeling sick; heat cramps; heat rash; heat oedema; heat exhaustion and heatstroke. • Increased numbers of admissions to hospital and consultations with GPs, and additional demands placed on emergency services. • Fatalities, particularly among the vulnerable and older people. The main causes of illness and death during a heatwave are exacerbation of respiratory and cardiovascular illness. Severe and extended heatwaves can also cause severe disruption to general city infrastructure and public services like transport, waste collection, wastewater management, water distribution, energy provision and the health services. The number of visitors in the city of Brighton & Hove rises sharply in the summer and during other major holidays. This can have an impact on the capacity of health services, especially during periods of intense heat. According to the Met Office's UKCP18 predictions (https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/binaries/content/assets/metofficegovuk/pdf/research/ukcp/ukcp18-fact-sheet-derived-projections.pdf) summers are expected to be up to 5 degrees hotter in the South East between 2061 and 2080 - The probability of exceeding 30ºC for more than 2 days rises from typically once every 4 years now, to about four times every year by 2070s. Environmental risk factors for increased exposure to heat include living in urban areas. This can be due to the urban heat island, poor access to green space and/or housing of a type that overheats. One in five homes in England are prone to overheating (such as south-facing top-floor flats) and few (less than 3%) have air conditioning. Many of these environmental factors disproportionately affect those on lower incomes, and this group are also more likely to have increased exposure at work, for example working outdoors or on tasks that involve high temperatures. Climate Just have produced a heat vulnerability index which shows that there are areas in Brighton & Hove at relatively high risk within Whitehawk, Central Brighton, Moulsecoomb, Coldean and Stanmer (https://www.climatejust.org.uk/map.html). More work is needed to integrate results from our Urban Heat Island spatial analysis (2023), which takes into account additional environmental factors such as surface albedos, with Climate Just's Socio Spatial Heat Vulnerability Index.

An initial science-based Climate Change Risk Assessment for Sunderland has been developed, aligned with the UK Climate Risk Independent Assessment (CCRA3). The Risk Assessment has been considered by the Sunderland Health and Wellbeing Board and climate resilience now forms a core part of the revised Sunderland Healthy City Plan 2025-2025, which was adopted by Cabinet in July 2025 Meetings and Events . 
The risk assessment identifies climate risks across 4 categories, including those affecting public health. The Service area experts from Public Health who informed the Sunderland climate risk assessment have incorporated the risks within Sunderland's revised Healthy City Plan 2025/2035. These include risks to health and wellbeing from changes in air quality, extreme temperatures and flooding as well as the challenge of health inequalities. 
	
Sunderland's Climate Change Risk Assessment and Healthy City Plan 2025/2035 is informed by The Joint Strategic Needs Assessment (2023-24) which provides an overview of the demographics of Sunderland. Compared to England, the population of Sunderland has a higher proportion of older people who use health and social care services more intensively than any other population groups and may require more complex treatment due to frailty and the presence of one or more long term conditions. The population of Sunderland has a higher proportion of people aged 65 years and older (20.5%), compared to England's proportion (18.4%). The population aged 65 years and over is projected to rise to 24.7% by 2043. In addition, the JSNA demonstrates how health inequalities within Sunderland result in significant variations in mortality and life expectancy at birth between wards. Priority actions to reduce the risks identified and their impact will be taken forward as part of a strategic and co-ordinated approach to adaptation, working both locally and regionally as appropriate. 
Sunderland's public health services understand how they can and must support the proposed adaptation and mitigation recommendations within the Council's Risk Assessment and Action Plan. This is underpinned by the UK Health Security Agency's 'Health Effects of Climate Change' (HECC) report, which supported further understanding of the implications of climate change on our population's health and the resulting inequalities which may be created or perpetuated. Public health input into Sunderland's climate risk assessment work has suggested approaches to how best prepare and protect our most vulnerable communities from these inevitable risks.	

Sunderland City Council have forged a £240,000 citywide partnership with Groundwork North East & Cumbria Sunderland and Citizens Advice Sunderland to deliver an OFGEM/REDRESS-funded and Energy Saving Trust (EST) administered energy and retrofit advice programme to assist 3300 households via home visits, community events and telephone advice calls from February 2025 to March 2027. The project, entitled “Energy Savvy”, is delivered by Green Doctors from Groundwork NE&C who liaise directly with SCC Public Health Team and the citywide GP Alliance (GPA) so partner home-visiting health and social prescribers can refer privately owned and rented households with health conditions made worse by living in cold, mouldy and damp conditions. As part of the project Groundwork NE&C Sunderland also provide energy and retrofit advice training to health and social prescribers to ensure the Make Every Call Count (MECC) initiative is maximised. During Green Doctor visits, the property is also assessed for Warm Homes Local Grant and / or ECO4/GBIS eligibility which can lead to full or partial whole-house retrofit including solar panels, insulation and low carbon heating technologies such as Air Source Heat Pumps all of which serve to make a home more affordably warm and healthier.
As of August 2025, 300 small measures have been installed including LED bulbs, radiator panels and hydrometers. £2500 worth of incorrect billings have been identified and resolved while £1000 of bill savings have been generated.
