El cambio climático impacta de forma directa e indirecta la salud de la población y el funcionamiento de los servicios de salud en Montería. Los principales efectos identificados son:
Impactos en la salud de la población
1.	Enfermedades transmitidas por vectores
oEl aumento de las temperaturas y la variabilidad en las lluvias favorecen la reproducción del Aedes aegypti (mosquito transmisor del dengue, chikungunya y zika).
oEn Montería se han reportado incrementos cíclicos de casos de dengue en temporadas lluviosas y cálidas, lo que presiona la capacidad hospitalaria.
2.	Golpes de calor y enfermedades cardiovasculares/respiratorias
o	Las olas de calor frecuentes en la región Caribe incrementan el riesgo de deshidratación, golpes de calor, complicaciones cardiovasculares y crisis respiratorias.
o	Afectan especialmente a adultos mayores, niños y personas con enfermedades crónicas.
3.	Calidad del aire y enfermedades respiratorias
oLas altas temperaturas, combinadas con emisiones urbanas y polvo, agravan problemas de asma, EPOC y alergias.
4.	Seguridad alimentaria y nutrición
oSequías en la zona rural impactan cultivos y disponibilidad de alimentos, lo que puede afectar el estado nutricional de comunidades vulnerables.
oEl incremento en precios de alimentos genera inseguridad alimentaria en familias de bajos ingresos.
5.	Salud mental
oEventos extremos como inundaciones en la cuenca del Sinú o sequías severas generan estrés, ansiedad y traumas en las comunidades afectadas.

Impactos en los servicios de salud
1.	Aumento en la demanda de atención
oLos brotes de enfermedades vectoriales y los efectos del calor extremo generan picos de demanda en hospitales y centros de salud.
2.	Interrupciones por eventos extremos
oInundaciones urbanas y rurales pueden afectar la infraestructura hospitalaria, el transporte de pacientes y el acceso a insumos médicos.
oRiesgo de cortes de energía y agua en hospitales, que dependen de servicios básicos para operar.
3.	Presión financiera y operativa
oEl incremento en morbilidad relacionada con el clima exige más recursos para prevención, medicamentos, campañas de salud pública y capacidad hospitalaria.
4.	Vulnerabilidad del personal de salud
oMédicos y trabajadores del sector también están expuestos a golpes de calor, enfermedades vectoriales y dificultades logísticas durante emergencias climáticas.
Conclusión
En Montería, el cambio climático agrava los riesgos en salud pública (dengue, golpes de calor, desnutrición, problemas respiratorios y salud mental) y pone en tensión los servicios de salud debido a la mayor demanda, los daños por inundaciones/sequías y la necesidad de inversiones adicionales para garantizar continuidad y resiliencia en la atención.

Assim, considerando os diversos estudos que mostram a relação de determinantes ambientais e fatores climáticos sob a dinâmica das endemias, e conhecendo-se a pertinência e a magnitude da dengue no Brasil e no mundo, torna-se uma questão de saúde relevante para o município. column20: Com base nas informações fornecidas pela Secretaria de Saúde de Santo André, embora não existam estudos específicos que estabeleçam uma relação direta e formal entre mudanças climáticas e os impactos na saúde no município, a vigilância epidemiológica de rotina por meio de sistemas como o SINAN (Sistema de Informação de Agravos de Notificação) e a unidade sentinela de síndrome gripal na UPA Sacadura Cabral, permite identificar padrões sazonais e extremos climáticos que influenciam significativamente a saúde da população. Os três problemas principais selecionados: agravamento de doenças respiratórias, aumento de doenças transmitidas por vetores e água e sobrecarga do sistema de saúde, emergem como os mais críticos devido à consistência com que são observados em resposta a condições como clima seco, chuvas intensas seguidas de altas temperaturas e eventos de poluição atmosférica. Por exemplo, o clima seco e a instabilidade do ar intensificam crises de doenças respiratórias crônicas e agudas, enquanto chuvas fortes combinadas com calor elevado criam ambientes ideais para a proliferação do Aedes aegypti e surtos de dengue, além de elevar o risco de leptospirose e hepatite A através do contato com águas contaminadas. Esses fatores, por sua vez, resultam em uma demanda aumentada e por vezes sobrecarregada por serviços de saúde, afetando tanto a capacidade de resposta do sistema quanto o bem-estar da comunidade, mesmo que ainda não se disponha de uma modelagem climática detalhada que quantifique integralmente essas correlações.

Under continued warming in recent years, dengue fever vector mosquitoes have shown signs of spreading to central and northern Taiwan. Extreme rainfall has caused flooding in low-lying areas, providing breeding environments for these mosquitoes and accelerating their reproduction. The primary dengue fever vector in New Taipei City is the Aedes albopictus mosquito, which is mainly distributed in urban green spaces such as parks, schools, and organic vegetable gardens, as well as in suburban and rural green areas. Breeding sites include both artificial water containers and natural water-holding containers.

Dengue fever is clinically easy to confuse with COVID-19. After Taiwan reopened its borders in 2023, international travel increased, leading to a surge in COVID-19 cases, which also posed challenges to dengue fever control. According to statistics from the Taiwan Centers for Disease Control (CDC) under the Ministry of Health and Welfare, New Taipei City recorded 113 confirmed cases of dengue fever in 2024.

In response to local dengue fever outbreaks and related control needs, the New Taipei City Environmental Protection Department has implemented measures such as tracking confirmed cases' activities and contact histories, and working with health authorities to designate control zones for spraying and breeding site elimination. Specifically, 133 spraying zones were designated in high-risk bamboo forests in Wuliao Village and high-risk vegetable farms in the Baiji area of Sanxia District. More than 2,000 personnel were mobilized to eliminate breeding sources. To reduce mosquito breeding in bamboo forests, 11,000 bamboo sections were covered with protective bags.

Climate change is increasingly impacting both health outcomes and the capacity of health services in the jurisdiction of Çanakkale. Rising temperatures and the growing frequency of heatwaves have led to an increase in heat-related illnesses, particularly affecting vulnerable populations such as the elderly, children, and those with pre-existing conditions.

In addition, prolonged droughts and declining air quality are contributing to respiratory diseases such as asthma and COPD. There is also concern regarding the future spread of vector-borne diseases (e.g., tick-borne and mosquito-borne illnesses), although current incidence remains limited.

These climate-related health outcomes are putting additional strain on local health services, especially during seasonal peaks. Public health infrastructure must now incorporate climate resilience measures, including early warning systems, heat-health action plans, and awareness campaigns.

Çanakkale Municipality is working to integrate public health considerations into its climate adaptation and disaster preparedness strategies to ensure long-term community well-being.

column20: Para conocer más sobre el impacto en la salud humana por los peligros relacionados al clima, se realizó un estudio para el análisis y la identificación de las Islas de Calor en el cantón (Se cuenta con mapas que identifican tanto las islas de calor con la caracterización vegetal del cantón de La Unión).Se cuenta con un análisis realizado durante el 2020, sobre las islas de calor, las cuales están asociadas al daño a la salud pública al disminuir la calidad del aire, además, las islas de calor pueden reducir la calidad del agua mediante la contaminación térmica. Las Islas de Calor, al igual que las superficies calientes en las zonas urbanas calientan el aire ambiente, también transfieren calor a las aguas pluviales. Los distritos de Concepción, San Juan, San Diego y Tres Ríos presentan importantes islas de calor las cuales en la figura corresponde al color más intenso y a las regiones con mayor desarrollo de infraestructura gris. El distrito con el mayor rango de variación es San Rafael y el distrito con la mayor temperatura superficial del terreno es San Juan y los distritos con menor cantidad de islas de calor son Dulce Nombre y San Ramón.El calor urbano ya está afectando a la salud humana, al tiempo que pueden incidir en el consumo de la energía y la contaminación ambiental. La reducción de las islas de calor urbano puede tanto mitigar el cambio climático (reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero) como adaptarse al cambio climático (prepararse para los impactos inevitables del cambio climático). La exposición a altas temperaturas puede provocar insolación, agotamiento por calor, calambres por calor, sarpullido por calor y malestar general. La gravedad de las enfermedades relacionadas con el calor también aumenta con la edad: \'Los calambres por calor en una persona de 17 años pueden ser un agotamiento por calor en una persona de 40 años y un golpe de calor en una persona mayor de 60\' .Las personas de edad con ingresos fijos, junto con otras personas de bajos ingresos, tienen menos capacidad para pagar el recibo por energía eléctrica que por lo general aumenta por el uso de ventiladores o aires acondicionados para contrarrestar el calor, lo que las hace más vulnerables. Los lactantes, los niños y los residentes socialmente aislados corren un riesgo especial de sucumbir a las enfermedades relacionadas con el calor. Los trabajadores a la intemperie, los discapacitados mentales, las personas sin hogar y los que padecen ciertas afecciones crónicas también son más vulnerables al calor que el residente medio.Las islas de calor dañan la salud pública al disminuir la calidad del aire. La combinación del aumento de la contaminación y las temperaturas más altas da lugar a más smog (ozono a nivel del suelo). El smog agrava las enfermedades respiratorias como el asma, que son más frecuentes entre los mismos grupos que ya son vulnerables a las enfermedades relacionadas con el calor: los ancianos, los niños pequeños, los pobres y las personas con enfermedades crónicas preexistentes . Además, las islas de calor pueden reducir la calidad del agua mediante la contaminación térmica. Al igual que las superficies calientes en las zonas urbanas calientan el aire ambiente, también transfieren calor a las aguas pluviales.Los ecosistemas urbanos y la diversidad biológica desempeñan un papel cada vez más importante en la ayuda a las ciudades para que se adapten al cambio climático. El aprovechamiento de la biodiversidad y los ecosistemas urbanos como soluciones de adaptación y mitigación ayudará a lograr resultados más resistentes, sostenibles y habitables.

In Vijayawada, climate change is increasing the number of extreme heat days and humid conditions along the Krishna River floodplain, increasing heat‑related illness and dehydration, while intensifying monsoon variability raises flood risk, triggering injuries, vector-borne and water‑borne diseases, and service disruptions to hospitals and urban primary health centers.

Public health facilities are widely distributed throughout Vijayawada city, providing affordable health care services to 82.5% of the population within a 1 km radius. Further, considering that slum dwellers primarily avail the affordable public
health care services, overlaying slums with the public health care accessibility map shows that ~99% of slum dwellers can access such facilities within a 1 km distance. Only about 1% of slum dwellers are located more than 1 km away from public health care facilities. Hence, the health system is considered an important supporting factor to raise the adaptive capacity of the city's population.

column20: Con la crisis sanitaria del coronavirus se ha demostrado la poca cobertura de las redes de salud para dar abasto ante una emergencia. Pese a que Chile está adscrita a la red de aprendizaje de la Cepal, y forma parte del análisis y acciones de adaptación del reporte de la \'adaptación al cambio climático en megaciudades de américa latina\' del mismo organismo, se identifican varios problemas de gestión de salud pública a nivel comunal, ya que Providencia no cuenta con un informe actualizado sobre los impactos en la salud pública ante el cambio climático. En el 2017, el Ministerio del Medio Ambiente en conjunto con el Ministerio de salud, pusieron en marcha un Plan de Adaptación al Cambio Climático en el sector salud para las distintas regiones del país, en la cual se pretende monitorear y actualizar los indicadores de distintos fenómenos a nivel local, para fortalecer los distintos puntos de salud y generar mejores planes de manejo y adaptación frente a cualquier amenaza del CC. Sin embargo, la información no está actualizada a nivel comunal, por lo que no se puede estimar el avance ni estado de este plan. La comuna de Providencia cuenta con 8 centros de salud, entre los cuales destacan hospitales, institutos y centros de salud familiar, y según el PLADECO (2013-2021), identifica a la población en proceso de envejecimiento, problemas de salud mental y de alimentación, como los más urgentes y vulnerables. Además, no toda la población de providencia cuenta con coberturas de seguro médico o acceso gratuito e integral a éstos.

Lyme disease has been detected with regularity with Island Health's service delivery area, but the incidence of locally acquired cases remains very low.  O controle vetorial de Aedes aegypti acontece continuamente por meio de ações e visitas bimestrais (que compreende os ciclos de visitação) realizadas pelos Agentes de Combate às Endemias (ACE) nos imóveis, terrenos baldios, pontos estratégicos e afins, com ações de orientação em educação e combate ao mosquito Aedes aegypt, de forma intersetorial em com setores administrativos como Secretaria do Urbanismo, Habitação e Meio Ambiente-Seuma; a Agência Municipal do Meio Ambiente-AMA e a Secretaria da Conservação e Serviços Públicos-SESEP. column20: Critical infrastructures owned or managed by the Town of Bridgewater are necessary for maintaining basic health and safety in the community, and for ensuring the normal functioning of the community and its economy. Multiple infrastructures have been assessed as being at least moderately at risk of significant impact by climate change, and the following have been assessed as being highly at risk: fire protection (hydrants), combined sanitary and storm sewers, sanitary sewer lift stations and pumps, and LaHave River bridges (owned by the Province of Nova Scotia). Compromise or damage of these critical infrastructures would result in significant problems for the community, including considerable health and safety risks, compromised ability to respond to emergencies, and wide-scale economic disruption. Currently few if any adaptation plans exist to mitigate these potential impacts, and in many cases the full extent of the impacts is not properly understood. Through consultations with emergency response professionals, it has become clear that emergency services (fire, police, EHS, Red Cross, public works, and health care services) will quickly become overwhelmed if a significant extreme weather event were to hit Bridgewater or nearby communities. These resources are often already stretched handling routine emergency situations, and the toll on these services would be extreme if a situation arose where there were multiple deaths, injuries, fires, isolated populations, hazardous material spills, etc., compounded by blocked streets and damaged infrastructure. While basic emergency response protocols and procedures are in place, sheer overwhelm is a situation that is typically not planned for, and collective response capacity among several compromised services is relatively unknown. A lack of ability to provide functional emergency services during an extreme weather event exposes the community to significant risk of injury and loss of life, as well as property damage and disruption to community functioning. Vulnerable populations would be particularly at risk, as their emergency response and care needs are higher than for other segments of the population.

Hasta el momento, en la comuna de Punta Arenas los resultados de salud no se analizan explícitamente desde la perspectiva del cambio climático, lo que refleja un vacío de conocimiento y de información sistematizada sobre esta relación. Sin embargo, es importante reconocer que los impactos del clima extremo propio de la zona, sumados a las proyecciones de variabilidad climática, ya están condicionando la salud de la población. Entre los posibles efectos destacan el aumento de enfermedades respiratorias y cardiovasculares asociadas a bajas temperaturas y a la contaminación atmosférica por el uso intensivo de combustibles térmicos, así como riesgos para la salud mental vinculados al aislamiento geográfico, eventos climáticos adversos y estrés por emergencias.

En materia de servicios, el sistema de salud local enfrenta desafíos de preparación y resiliencia, especialmente frente a una eventual mayor frecuencia de emergencias climáticas (temporal de nieve, inundaciones costeras o vientos extremos), que pueden interrumpir la continuidad de la atención, limitar el acceso a centros de salud o aumentar la demanda de consultas.

La implementación del Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC) representa una oportunidad para avanzar en la integración de la dimensión climática en la gestión de salud, mediante la generación de estudios específicos, campañas de sensibilización comunitaria, y el fortalecimiento de la coordinación con la red de salud para anticipar riesgos y proteger a la población más vulnerable (niños, adultos mayores y personas con enfermedades crónicas).

column20: A nivel de Región Metropolitana de Santiago, se sabe que el cambio climático tiene un impacto sobre la salud de las personas, y se están haciendo actividades para subsanar dichos impactos. Sin embargo, a nivel de jurisdicción, no se han cuantificado los impactos a nivel salud ni se disponen de indicadores cuantitativos para la medición de éstos. Sí se puede informar respecto a la vulnerabilidad de las personas. En el Registro Social de Hogares, existen 5582 vecinos de la comuna identificados. Este Registro corresponde al 40-60% de menores ingresos y mayor grado de vulnerabilidad. Estas personas reciben una serie de ayudas sociales en momentos de eventos críticos derivados del cambio climático.\n\nEn el análisis de vulnerabilidad, se encontró que el aumento de temperaturas, escasez hídrica, incendios e inundaciones son las amenazas que mayor impacto tienen en la salud humana. Estas amenazas afectan principalmente a los grupos vulnerables identificados. Sin embargo, al mismo tiempo, la comuna cuenta con indicadores muy altos de resiliencia, donde se destacan la cantidad de médicos en salud primaria, planificación municipal en torno a la gestión de riesgos, y la superficie de áreas verdes.

L'ensemble de ces facteurs se répercuteront sur les inégalités sociales de santé du territoire de la Métropole. column20: The primary health threats to Miami-Dade County with respect to climate change are extreme heat and extreme weather events. With respect to heat, extreme heat is already a danger to vulnerable community members throughout the County, particular those with health predispositions (age, pre-existing conditions, etc.). Miami's hot and humid climate can be a stressor and health burden for residents exposed to heat, especially in the summer months. As temperatures continually warm with climate change, people will be at greater risk to adverse heat health impacts. Looking to the future, if greenhouse gas emissions continue without mitigation, Miami-Dade is projected to have 14 \'off the chart\' heat index days by late century (2070-2099). \'Off the chart\' is considered a value of over 135०F. Health risks associated with extreme heat are expected to be more common as the climate continues to grow more hot and humid. In Miami by mid-century, it is likely that a total of 88 days, or roughly three months of the year, will have a heat index of 105℉ or greater ( Southeast Florida Climate Compact ). All people in Miami-Dade are at risk, but some groups are more sensitive than others. High-risk groups for heat related illnesses include adults over 65 years, young children, pregnant women, lower-income populations, outdoor workers, people recreating outside, athletes, and people with pre-existing (heart, lung, kidney) conditions who take certain medications that reduce their body's ability to keep cool.Heat has a strong overlap in its effects with increasing respiratory and health issues, as well as allergens. In addition, mosquito- and vector-borne diseases are likely to become more common with rising temperatures. Finally, hurricanes and similar extreme weather events are more like short-term shocks to the system rather than chronic stresses, and depending on their frequency and intensity, and overlap with extreme heat, they threaten critical infrastructure and complicate emergency health service delivery.

Penyakit Menular
Peningkatan kasus Diare, Demam Berdarah Dengue (DBD), Malaria, dan Infeksi Saluran Pernapasan Akut (ISPA) akibat perubahan pola curah hujan, suhu, serta genangan banjir

Akses terhadap air minum layak dan sanitasi aman sangat rentan karena perubahan iklim memperburuk kualitas sumber air, memperbesar risiko banjir, dan meningkatkan penyebaran penyakit berbasis air

Gizi dan Ketahanan Pangan
Perubahan iklim mengancam ketersediaan pangan, berdampak pada stunting dan malnutrisi pada balita. RPJMD menekankan program penurunan prevalensi stunting lintas sektor sebagai respon terhadap kerentanan ini

Kesehatan Ibu, Anak, dan Lansia
Kelompok rentan (ibu hamil, balita, lansia) lebih berisiko terdampak penyakit dan gangguan kesehatan akibat gelombang panas, banjir, dan kekurangan gizi

Kesehatan Reproduksi
Perubahan iklim masuk sebagai faktor risiko dalam program kesehatan reproduksi, terutama terkait kesehatan ibu, KB, serta remaja di wilayah rawan bencana

The municipality has a designated cooling center (the James Harmon Community Center) which is handicap accessible and has restrooms, a kitchen with running water, bathrooms, air conditioning, free charging and wi-fi capacity, and a backup generator. The typical operating hours of the cooling center are 9 am to 4:30 pm - however on Thursday availability of the cooling center extends beyond typical business hours to 8 pm and the facility has remote opening and closing options should residents need emergency access out of office hours. During heat emergencies the municipal pool is also available to residents at guest fee prices (i.e. those who do not have annual summer pool memberships) and there is a splash pool for children. Free wi-fi is also offered at the pool. In 2019, Hastings-on-Hudson reviewed its heat emergency protocols and assessed the adequacy of its cooling centers. Several improvements were made, including updating the Villages “Are You OK” list (which is used to check in on seniors during and after heat, storm or snow emergencies), extending the hours of the cooling center, identifying local transportation options to make the cooling center more accessible and available, more effectively promoting awareness of the cooling center in the community, and committing to track usage. In 2021, the municipality began to actively promote the availability of its cooling center and now tracks utilization of the cooling center on hot days.

column20: Antalya is one of the provinces with the highest number of storms and tornadoes in Turkey, but it is also affected by high temperatures, especially in summer. Therefore, it is essential to take precautions knowing that the effects of climate change will create more risks in certain areas and population groups. It is clear that there has not been a detailed study on the direct effects of climate change on public health in the city, but there is a need for such a detailed study on extreme weather events. In the report prepared by AFAD in 2021, the number of vulnerable population groups was determined based on data from the Provincial Directorate of Family and Social Services. The ratio of the number of people with severe disabilities and in need of care in Antalya was calculated as 0.92. Although this rate remains low compared to the population, the number of vulnerable population in Kepez, Muratpaşa, Alanya and Manavgat districts varies between 1000 and 4000. Although climate change will affect the entire city, its impact on the vulnerable population will be much more devastating. For this reason, the development of climate change adaptation strategies should first be developed for the areas where these populations live predominantly and then should be generalized throughout the city. Antalya is a city that encounters climatic disasters quite frequently. Both its geographical structure and climate structure cause the city to have many and varied weather events. In addition to these, the fact that the climatic situation is changing day by day and the earth's temperature is increasing leads to the frequency and intensity of climatic disasters. In Antalya, floods, landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and heavy snowfall, earthquakes, fires, storms and tornadoes, heat waves and frost are observed. Due to the fact that Antalya is the 5th largest province of the country and the risks it faces, Antalya Provincial Disaster and Emergency Directorate (Antalya AFAD) was established with the law in 2009. There is also growing concern over the rise in vector-borne diseases like West Nile virus and leishmaniasis, exacerbated by changing precipitation and temperature regimes. The municipality collaborates with the İl Sağlık Müdürlüğü (Provincial Health Directorate) for syndromic surveillance and heatwave warnings but lacks systematic health impact assessments due to limited technical capacity and financing.

Os eventos de temperaturas elevadas / ondas de calor apresentam contornos gravosos, com impactes relevantes e transversais do ponto de vista sectorial. Considerando o panorama descrito, a vulnerabilidade individual e coletiva tenderá a aumentar, prevendo-se que o quotidiano da população seja afetado. Neste contexto, enumeram-se como principais impactes: aumento da probabilidade de ocorrência de incêndios rurais; danos para as infraestruturas (e.g. degradação devido ao calor excessivo); danos para a saúde, particularmente nas faixas etárias mais vulneráveis (crianças e idosos); alterações no uso de equipamentos e serviços (e.g. aumento do consumo de água e energia; sobrecarga das unidades de saúde); danos para a vegetação (e.g. perda de coberto vegetal para a fixação do solo); diminuição do resgate de carbono; aumento das emissões de CO2; danos para a biodiversidade (e.g. alteração dos ecossistemas); aumento do custo de matérias-primas (e.g. madeira); aumento do custo associado ao dispositivo para o combate a incêndios; aumento das despesas na área da saúde. O fenómeno de precipitação intensa (cheias e inundações) manifesta particularmente impactes gravosos no território concelhio. No futuro, estes eventos tenderão a tornar-se menos frequentes, ainda que se conjeturem mais intensos, dada a projeção de aumento dos fenómenos extremos. Entre os principais impactes, diretos e indiretos, associados a tais ocorrências, referem-se danos para as infraestruturas (transporte, telecomunicações, drenagem de águas pluviais, etc.), danos em edifícios, inundações, alterações no uso de equipamentos e serviços, sobrecargas de infraestruturas viárias e de meios de transporte, aumento de custos de reparação/substituição de equipamentos e infraestruturas, danos para as cadeias de produção e necessidade de realojamento temporário de pessoas.

1.Air Quality & Respiratory Health
The Bradford Clean Air Plan, including a Clean Air Zone (CAZ), led to a 25% drop in respiratory-related primary care visits and a 24% drop in cardiovascular visits after implementation.
In addition the CAZ is starting to help alleviate financial pressures on health care sector through a reduction in the cost of patient care of £30,700 per month in it's first year.

https://borninbradford.nhs.uk/news/bradford-clean-air-zone-saves-nhs-over-30000-a-month-in-first-year/

Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) levels decreased by 11.5 μg/m³, with continued reductions post-implementation.

These improvements suggest that climate policies targeting emissions can directly reduce disease burden.

2. Heatwaves & Vulnerable Populations
Rising temperatures increase risks of heat-related illnesses, especially among the elderly, children, and those with chronic conditions.

Bradford's diverse population, including communities with higher rates of deprivation, may face disproportionate health risks due to limited access to cooling, green spaces, and healthcare.

3. Mental Health & Environmental Stress
Climate anxiety, displacement due to flooding, and disruption of services can exacerbate mental health conditions.

The district's health services are beginning to factor in climate resilience in mental health planning.

column20: Maintaining health and safety is Goal One of Fredericton's Climate Change Adaptation Plan. Climate change creates and heightens health and safety concerns for the public and for City staff and contractors. The City of Fredericton will do its part to maintain health and safety for its staff and for the public in the roles it previously has played, such as providing access to emergency services and providing updates on safety risks associated with flooding and extreme weather events. The City will work to enhance its services in these areas, including increasing communications and helping citizens to prepare themselves in advance of extreme weather.Below are some examples of how climate change may impact community health or the health system of our City:- Lyme disease is expected to become more prevalent as longer, hotter summers and more mild winters increase the ticks' rates of survival, growth and reproduction.- Climate change increases risk to mental and physical health and vulnerable populations may experience heightened risks in these areas.- Extreme heat can compound issues during emergency calls, including the exasperation of heath and mental health issues. Increases in frequency and duration of periods of extreme heat leads to increased health and safety risks for the public, especially vulnerable populations due to their limited ability to prepare for and cope with such events. There is expected to be more calls for service that could overwhelm emergency response. The combination of heat stress and poor air quality can pose a major health risk to vulnerable groups: young children, elderly, , economically disadvantaged, and those with preexisting health conditions.- Extreme weather events will lead to an increase in power outages and associated health and safety risks relating to lack of traffic signals, unsafe food preparation, unsafe heating practices, and lack of indoor heating and cooling.- Wildfires threaten lives directly and can cause health impacts, particularly respiratory impacts, from inhalation of particle pollution. Fires spread air pollution not only nearby, but thousands of kilometres away—causing breathing difficulties in even healthy individuals, but especially in children, older adults and those with heart disease, diabetes, asthma, COPD and other lung diseases.

The following are some of the key climate hazards that are affecting the region:

Heatwaves: Cornwall is already experiencing more frequent and intense heatwaves. These heatwaves can lead to heatstroke, dehydration, and other heat-related illnesses. The elderly, young children, and people with chronic health conditions are particularly vulnerable to these health effects.

Flooding: Cornwall is also at risk of flooding from sea level rise and more extreme storms. Flooding can cause injuries, respiratory problems, and waterborne illnesses. It can also disrupt access to healthcare services and damage essential infrastructure.

Air pollution: Cornwall's air quality is already poor, and climate change is making it worse. Air pollution can cause respiratory problems, heart disease, and cancer. It can also worsen the symptoms of existing health conditions.

Vector-borne diseases: Climate change is creating new opportunities for vector-borne diseases, such as Lyme disease and West Nile virus. These diseases can be transmitted through the bite of an infected insect.

The following are some of the health issues that are being driven by these climate hazards:

Heat-related illnesses: Heatstroke, dehydration, and other heat-related illnesses are becoming more common in Cornwall.

Respiratory problems: Air pollution is causing more respiratory problems, such as asthma and bronchitis.

Cardiovascular diseases: Climate change is increasing the risk of cardiovascular diseases, such as heart attacks and strokes.

Waterborne illnesses: Flooding can increase the risk of waterborne illnesses, such as cholera and typhoid fever.

Vector-borne diseases: Climate change is creating new opportunities for vector-borne diseases, such as Lyme disease and West Nile virus.The following are some of the vulnerable populations in Cornwall that are most affected by climate change:

The elderly: The elderly are more vulnerable to heat-related illnesses and other health effects of climate change.

Young children: Young children are also more vulnerable to heat-related illnesses and other health effects of climate change.

People with chronic health conditions: People with chronic health conditions, such as asthma and heart disease, are more vulnerable to the health effects of climate change.

Low-income households: Low-income households are more likely to live in areas that are vulnerable to climate change, such as floodplains. They are also less likely to have access to air conditioning or other resources that can help them cope with the effects of climate change.

column20: Prolonged periods of hot weather, and extreme hot days, can have a significant and detrimental impact on health of residents for a multitude of reasons, and these impacts are set to become even more significant if climate change continues unchecked. Certain meteorological conditions lead to a build up in toxins in the air we breathe (particulates and nitrogen dioxide being the two predominant toxins). The two major physical impacts from particulates are on the respiratory and cardiovascular systems, and there is emerging evidence that there may be links to degenerative neurological conditions such as dementia. It is estimated that between 28,000-36,000 deaths in the UK annually are linked to poor air quality. The cost of this in England between 2017 and 2025 is estimated to be as high as 5.56 billion. The West Midlands, being predominantly urban, also suffers from the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect. Research from the 2003 heat wave shows that the region had an estimated 90-130 excess deaths during this period. The UHI effect pushed average temperatures 3C higher than the neighbouring rural areas. It is suggested that the UHI contributed up to 52% of heat related mortality. During the 2003 heatwave, ambulance call outs in Birmingham increased by a third. Hospitals, care homes and other health centres in the West Midlands are ill-equipped to deal with extreme heat. Those in sub-standard housing, the elderly, and those from a lower socio-economic background are less likely to be able to adapt to these hot days, and are therefore more susceptible to illness during these periods. In addition, those with disabilities and pre-existing medical conditions are at a greater risk of complications arising from heat stress. It is also worth adding that the people experiencing homelessness in the West Midlands are also particularly vulnerable to these extreme temperatures. The transport network is also susceptible to disruption during hot weather, for example, railways often have to run at reduced speed. The heatwave in July 2022 where temperatures peaked 40 degrees nationally, the West Midlands felt the damage extreme heat can cause in terms of excess deaths, transport systems failing and wildfires.\n\nThe WMCA are working with the University of Birmingham, in a project called WM-Adapt, to develop its understanding of the lived experiences of high temperatures felt by the most vulnerable communities and wards in the region. This should enable to the WMCA to build its evidence base with qualitative data over the next few years, with more local insights on the effects of extreme heat on health and wellbeing.

column20: Our area is affected by river flooding, storms, heavy rainfall, and urban flooding, which have significant impacts on health in various aspects. Starting with waterborne and foodborne diseases, the most common ones include diarrhea and leptospirosis due to contact with contaminated floodwaters. This is especially true for low-income populations who often lack proper protective equipment and knowledge on how to cope with disasters. However, due to concerns for their property, they tend to wade through floodwaters, increasing their risk of infection. Furthermore, prolonged flooding also affects individuals with respiratory conditions, as inhaling mold spores and harmful substances from floodwaters can worsen symptoms of asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Regarding accidents, floods and storms increase the risk of physical injuries, such as drowning or injury from debris swept by the flood, raising the likelihood of accidents during disasters. Mental health problems are also a significant concern, particularly for vulnerable populations, such as the elderly or those who lose their homes and property during floods. The stress from losing housing and the difficulties in recovery after a disaster can lead to anxiety, depression, and other mental health issues.

Accessibility to healthcare infrastructure is vital for enhancing living conditions and reducing vulnerability to extreme events such as climate-related disasters. Vulnerable groups, such as slum dwellers and people with special needs, often face heightened risks due to limited access to essential services like emergency healthcare, public transport, and green spaces.

In Bhavnagar, healthcare accessibility has been evaluated using spatial analysis, aligned with the Urban and Regional Development Plan Formulation and Implementation (URDPFI) guidelines. The analysis also correlates hospital locations with urban flood-prone areas to identify regions where accessibility is hindered due to waterlogging or flooding. Out of the city's 21 hospitals, 6 are impacted by urban floods.

Bhavnagar has a total of 1,459 hospital beds, which equates to 1.8 beds per 1,000 people, falling short of the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommendation of 3 beds per 1,000 people. Despite this, 95.9% of Bhavnagar's population (about 0.77 million people) can access healthcare services within a 3 km radius. However, slum dwellers, particularly in areas like Chitra and Fulsar, must travel more than 4.5 km to reach government healthcare facilities, placing them at higher risk during extreme events like heat waves and urban flooding.

In terms of spatial accessibility, the analysis reveals that:
•	52.6% of the population (0.42 million people) are within 1 km of healthcare facilities.
•	33.2% (0.27 million people) are within 1-2 km.
•	10% (81,000 people) are within 2-3 km.
For slum dwellers:
•	42% (39,000 people) are within 1 km.
•	43.6% (38,000 people) are within 1-2 km.
•	7.8% (7,000 people) are within 2-3 km.

Additionally, 4.1% of Bhavnagar's total population (around 33,000 people) and 7% of slum dwellers (about 6,000 people) live in areas where accessing healthcare facilities is challenging due to distance.

Further details can be found in section 3.7.2 of the Bhavnagar Climate Resilient City Action Plan (pages 56-58).

column20: London faces a steeply rising water deficit, projected to reach 400M litres per year by 2040. Over 25% of London's water supply is from high-risk sources, and distribution networks have an almost 25% leakage rate. Water scarcity and drought risks are not evenly distributed, with those in high-rise buildings, frequently in lower socio-economic status groups, particularly adversely affected. Heat-related deaths in the UK are projected to rise 500% to over 12,000 by 2080, with 3,271 excess deaths recorded in the UK by the Office for National Statistics during the 2022 heatwaves. Being densely built, H&F is particularly vulnerable. With only 28% green space coverage compared to 50% for London overall, H&F is subject to strong urban heat island (UHI) effects, in which urban areas can be up to 10°C warmer than surrounding areas. Extreme heat is expected to have particularly negative health impacts on older people and those with underlying health conditions, with up to an estimated 21 fatalities and 107 casualties in Hammersmith & Fulham in the event of a 2-week heatwave, based on borough-scaled estimates in the London Risk Register. Deaths from cardiovascular and respiratory diseases increase with hotter and colder temperatures, and heat-related illnesses (heat cramps, heat exhaustion and heat stroke) increase during heatwaves. Impacts are likely to be worst in the private rented sector as this has the most energy-inefficient housing, with households on lower incomes more likely to rent. Socioeconomic factors above such as underlying health conditions, low income, and tenancy status are unevenly distributed between communities and likely to be higher risk among some minority communities. Increased temperatures and cloud-free days may lead to increases in skin cancer and other UV-related illnesses. Flooding presents an immediate risk to life and injury from drowning, physical trauma, and issues relating to contaminated water. Flooding's most significant health burden in the UK relates to mental health. Mental health impacts can be short or long term, 'ranging from effects on wellbeing and stress or anxiety, to more severe mental health impacts which are characterised by clinical symptomatology and which require specialist health interventions' (UK Health Security Agency). A 2014 study by Public Health England found that 'people whose homes had been flooded were up to 6 times more likely to have probable PTSD, depression and/or anxiety than people who had not been flooded'. Climate risks also disrupt health-related services. Flooding and extreme heat can lead to transport-related impacts to the health system, impeding access to and for health services from impassable roads, melted highways surfaces, buckled rails, and failing vehicles. Flooding and extreme heat can also affect health infrastructure including electrical transmission and IT systems. Guy's and St Thomas's Hospital in London declared a critical incident on 19th July 2022 when record heat disabled 2 data centres disrupting access to critical clinical IT systems, with an estimated cost of £1.4m. The London Environment Strategy identifies a knock-on risk from power outages to the ability to pump clean water. 46% of food consumed in the UK is imported (United Kingdom Food Security Report 2021). Global climate risks to food production can increase the cost and reduce the availability of food in the UK, increasing food insecurity.

column20: As temperatures rise, the city will likely experience an increase in heat-related illnesses such as heat exhaustion and heatstroke, particularly among vulnerable populations like the elderly, young children, and those with pre-existing health conditions. In addition to heat, poor air quality may worsen due to higher concentrations of ground-level ozone, exacerbating respiratory conditions like asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Longer pollen seasons could also lead to an increase in allergies and asthma attacks. Furthermore, warmer temperatures and changing precipitation patterns could extend the breeding seasons for mosquitoes and other vectors, heightening the risk of vector-borne diseases such as West Nile virus, Zika, and dengue fever. Gainesville's subtropical climate makes it particularly susceptible to these changes. The city is also at risk of increased flooding and water contamination due to more frequent and severe storms, which could lead to a rise in waterborne diseases and contamination of drinking water. These environmental changes, along with the disruptions caused by extreme weather events like hurricanes, can have significant mental health impacts, contributing to stress, anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Environmental change may also disrupt local agriculture, affecting food security and nutrition, particularly for low-income populations. The combination of increased demand for healthcare services due to these issues can strain Gainesville's healthcare system, potentially leading to longer wait times and reduced access to care. Additionally, as certain areas become less habitable, Gainesville could see an influx of refugees, further straining local resources, including healthcare, housing, and social services. To mitigate these impacts, Gainesville will need to implement adaptation strategies such as enhancing public health surveillance, improving infrastructure, promoting green spaces, and educating the public about the associated health risks. By taking proactive steps, the city can better protect its residents from the health risks posed by a changing world.

column20: As temperatures rise, the incidence of heat-related illnesses, such as heat exhaustion and heatstroke, is expected to increase, leading to more emergency room visits and hospital admissions. The healthcare system may also see a rise in respiratory issues due to worsening air quality, as higher temperatures can increase the concentration of ground-level ozone and extend pollen seasons. This could result in more cases of asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and other respiratory conditions, further burdening healthcare facilities. The spread of vector-borne diseases, such as West Nile virus, Zika, and dengue fever, could become more prevalent as warmer temperatures and altered precipitation patterns create more favorable conditions for mosquitoes and other disease-carrying insects. This would not only increase the caseload for healthcare providers but also require additional resources for disease monitoring, prevention, and treatment efforts. Flooding and extreme weather events, which are expected to become more frequent and severe, pose a significant risk to Gainesville's health infrastructure. Floods can damage healthcare facilities, disrupt services, and lead to the contamination of water supplies, increasing the incidence of waterborne diseases. Hospitals and clinics may also face challenges in maintaining operations during and after extreme weather events, particularly if infrastructure is compromised. Mental health services are likely to come under increased strain, such as stress, anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), become more prevalent. The stress associated with extreme weather events, displacement, and the uncertainty of living in a changing world can have significant mental health repercussions, leading to greater demand for counseling and psychiatric services. The increased demand for healthcare services across multiple fronts—emergency care, respiratory treatment, disease prevention, mental health support—could stretch Gainesville's healthcare system thin. This strain might lead to longer wait times, reduced access to non-emergency care, and overall decreased quality of care. Furthermore, as hurricanes and the like potentially displaces populations, Gainesville could experience an influx of refugees, further overwhelming healthcare resources. To adapt to these challenges, Gainesville's health systems will need to invest in resilience by improving infrastructure, expanding capacity, enhancing emergency preparedness, and developing robust public health surveillance systems. Additionally, integrating resiliency planning into health planning and policy will be crucial to ensure the city's healthcare system can continue to provide high-quality care in the face of growing challenges.

In July 2023, Public Health Wales published a Health Impact Assessment (HIA) of Climate Change in Wales. HIA of climate change in Wales is a high-level, evidence-based strategic overview of the main health and wellbeing impacts of climate change in Wales. The HIA aims to support a range of agencies to enhance action on climate adaptation and resilience in Wales by providing evidence on the health, wellbeing and equity impacts of climate change in Wales, and what it means for people's lives in the places they live, work, learn and play. This includes economic, social, environmental and mental wellbeing. The HIA provides evidence to inform action on health and wellbeing for a wide range of stakeholders including: • Policy and decision makers across departments in national and local government • Local Health Boards and clinicians • Multisector partnerships like Public Services Boards and Local Resilience Fora • Environment sector, transport and other infrastructure agencies • Education, social care, community organisations and civil society.

column20: The Public Health Wales HIA Climate Change identified the following impacts on population health and equity; Climate change is complex and is an important determinant of health and wellbeing. Climate change does not exist in a vacuum and is caused and can be mitigated by, a wide range of international policies and political actors, as much as national, subnational and individual actions. Wales has control over some important policy levers and drivers to create action for climate change and health but not for others for example, the carbon emissions of other states and international trade, which also impact on the health and wellbeing of the Welsh population. 2. Climate change will have potential major, multifaceted, co-occurring and inequitable impacts across a range of determinants of health for example, nutrition and food security, community resilience and cohesion, displacement of people, access to healthcare, damage to housing, transport and infrastructure, environmental determinants including water supply, biodiversity and the economy. 3. Climate change will impact on the health and wellbeing of the whole population of Wales, and some population groups are likely to experience disproportionate negative impacts. For example, those on low incomes, children and young people, older adults, farmers, fishers and those who live in coastal areas. Settings such as education, workplaces, and health and social care facilities are also impacted by climate change and extreme weather events. Therefore, population and place-based vulnerability should be integrated into adaptation and resilience planning as much as sectoral and service-based risks. 4. There are a number of compounding and cumulative impacts on some population groups in Wales arising from climate change, Brexit, the ongoing impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the current cost of living crisis. 5. The impact on mental wellbeing should be explicitly considered as part of climate change plans and adaptation. Anxiety about the future, sense of control, democratic participation, and trauma from extreme weather and flooding are key factors influencing mental health and wellbeing.

column20: El plan de salud de la comuna de Renca se basa en la política nacional de fortalecimiento de la Atención Primaria de Salud orientada a mejorar resultados sanitarios, eficiencia, satisfacción usuaria y minimizar el efecto de los determinantes sociales de la salud. Esta política define al modelo de atención integral, familiar y comunitario, basado en un enfoque de derechos, como la forma más efectiva de dar respuesta a las necesidades y expectativas en salud de la población. Centrado en la persona y su familia, basado en el trabajo en equipos multidisciplinarios a cargo de poblaciones pequeñas, reconoce el valor del vínculo y de sistemas de cuidados a través del tiempo, y entiende el proceso salud enfermedad como un continuo, lo que permite implementar acciones para la promoción de la salud, reforzando la educación en factores protectores y prevención de factores de riesgo, desde un enfoque poblacional, y de esta forma se anticipa al daño. Cuenta con una red de establecimientos de Atención Primaria de Salud: 4 Centros de Salud Familiar -CESFAM- y 3 CESCOS (Pertenecientes al CESFAM Renca), 2 SAR, 1 SAPU, 3 Centros de rehabilitación de Base Comunitaria (RBC), 1 centro para NNAs de Salud Mental y 2 COSAM, para brindar atención al 83% de la población inscrita validada por FONASA. Sus 4 Centros de Salud se encuentran certificados por el Servicio de Salud Metropolitano Occidente -SSMOC- como Centros de Salud Familiar.Es así como enfrentamos los años 2021 y 2022 en donde tuvimos que sostener como red de salud las atenciones de pacientes con COVID, la vacunación COVID -19 y las atenciones regulares de nuestros establecimientos, intencionando en cada una de estas acciones la búsqueda constante de la innovación para poder dar una mejor respuesta y ampliar nuestras capacidades.Se instala el programa “Renca Contigo” como una nueva forma de enfrentar los problemas de salud mental, la “Unidad Rehabilitación post COVID” para atención de nuestros vecinos con secuelas respiratorias y motoras post COVID, la estrategia “Renca Agenda Fácil” como una nueva forma de agendamiento y la apertura de un nuevo canal de acceso a través de una línea 800 para agendamiento de horas de morbilidad. La implementación de agendamiento vía web y de Telesalud en los 4 centros de salud, entre otros, nos ha permitido que podamos retomar las atenciones habituales de nuestros establecimiento y que nuestros vecinos de una manera fácil y a distancia puedan obtener sus horas, y en muchas ocasiones a través de Telesalud , una solución a sus necesidades disminuyendo de forma importante la asistencia de usuarios a los centros de salud. Por último, nuestra “Unidad de gestión de Datos” que nos permite entre otras cosas, tener una mejor vigilancia sobre la eficiencia de nuestras atenciones de salud, información que nos orienta y ayuda a crear estrategias orientadas a disminuir el número de personas que no se presentan, y con esto eficientar el uso de las horas disponibles.El año 2022, las acciones en el área de salud, dieron como resultado:A nivel de infraestructura, se realizaron mejoras en el Cesfam Huamachuco en las áreas de vacunatorio , salas de ginecología, salas ERA /IRA , toma de muestra , podología, pasillos y rampas de acceso con una inversión de $72.969.992 mediante un PRAPS . En materia COVID-19, el año 2022 de mantuvo la estrategia Centinela Renca, con equipo multidisciplinario exclusivo para estas funciones compuesto por xxx funcionarios. Para la ejecución de la estrategia se implementó un centro de trazabilidad exclusivo fuera de los establecimientos de salud y se realizaron operativos búsqueda activa COVID durante todo el año 2022. Se realizaron operativos de búsqueda activa de casos COVID en escuelas y en los centros de salud.

column20: De acuerdo al último corte del mes de septiembre de 2022 la población percapitada en la comuna fue de 134.866 personas, lo que corresponde al 83% de la población estimada por el INE para el año 2021 que se atiende en los centros de salud . Por otro lado, Renca es considerada la 17° comuna de “media alta prioridad social” entre un total de 52 comunas de la Región Metropolitana, esto según el Índice de Prioridad Social (IPS) elaborado por la Secretaría Regional Ministerial de Desarrollo Social del año 2022.Según Censo 2017 significaba que Renca pasó de tener 35,49 adultos mayores por cada 100 menores de 15 años a tener 63,66 adultos mayores por cada 100 menores de 15 años. Sin duda un aumento sostenido que refuerza el hecho que la población de la comuna de Renca, en promedio ha ido progresivamente envejeciendo en los últimos 15 años. Según Naciones Unidas, una población envejecida es aquella en la que, del total de sus habitantes, más de un 7% son personas mayores de 65 años. De acuerdo a ello, ya Renca en el 2017 tiene una población envejecida de un 10%, lo que trae consigo, un incremento de las demandas en razón a las necesidades de este grupo etario altamente vulnerable, fundamentalmente de salud, económicas y sociales.De las consultas de morbilidad de niños y niñas entre los 0 a los 9 años, en el año 2022, las tres primeras causas de consulta están asociadas a consultas por otras morbilidades, otras morbilidades de tipo respiratorio y consultas por Infección respiratoria aguda (IRA) alta. En comparación con los años 2020 y 2021, donde las tres primeras causas de consultas de morbilidad son por este mismo tipo de atención. Durante el año 2022 existió un aumento significativo de las consultas de morbilidad infantil en la comuna que se puede atribuir a la disminución de restricciones de aforos y atenciones en los CESFAM. Por otro lado, la apertura de Jardines y Colegios logró un aumento de contagio de enfermedades entre niños y niñas. Del total de 115.003 consultas de morbilidad realizadas durante el año 2021, el 16,9% corresponde a personas mayores de 65 años. Mientras que en el año 2022 (corte agosto) esta cifra alcanza 95.817 consultas, lo que representa un 16,6%.En la comuna se busca implementar un modelo de atención basado en el concepto de envejecimiento activo y saludable, sustentado en un enfoque epidemiológico, en la estrategia de atención primaria, la promoción de la salud y el reconocimiento de los derechos de las personas mayores, con el objetivo de superar las actuales barreras de acceso a los servicios de salud, mantener la funcionalidad y reducir la discapacidad, morbilidad y mortalidad por causas evitables.Desde el punto de vista preventivo, se ha retomado la realización de EMPAM, teniendo el desafío de mejorar la cobertura de este examen preventivo en las personas mayores de la comuna. De la misma forma, durante el presente año se ha logrado retomar la totalidad de los talleres del programa Más Adultos Mayores Autovalentes de forma presencial, los que producto de la pandemia durante los años 2020 y 2021, tuvieron que adaptarse a otras estrategias como la modalidad remota a través de Zoom o entrega de cuadernillos en domicilio y seguimiento telefónico. Sumado a lo anterior, los equipos están velando por el acceso expedito de las personas mayores a las atenciones de salud, si bien actualmente existe una modernización de los sistemas para la toma de hora como lo son por teléfono o vía web, se mantiene un horario protegido para la solicitud de horas presenciales para los mayores de 60 años, en concordancia con la Ley 20.584 (Derechos y Deberes del Paciente).Producto de la necesidad de mantener los controles cardiovasculares de la población mayor durante la pandemia nace la estrategia 75+ mediante visitas domiciliarias para las personas mayores de 75 años, que producto de la pandemia y las distintas restricciones sanitarias vieron mermados sus controles de salud, considerando además que era una población susceptible de enfermar y tener graves complicaciones asociadas al Covid-19. Sumado a esto, se contempla el despacho de medicamentos crónicos para este grupo etario, lo cual ya se había comenzado a realizar desde mayo de 2020, y posteriormente se incluye también el despacho de los alimentos del Programa de Alimentación Complementaria del Adulto Mayor (PACAM). El programa ha sido bien valorado en la población beneficiaria y sus familias, generando altos niveles de satisfacción usuaria, en especial lo relacionado al despacho de medicamentos y PACAM.. Por lo anteriormente descrito se define mantener la estrategia de despacho de medicamento y PNAC en domiclio durante el año 2022 . Todas las prestaciones de salud se retomaron en los centros de salud durante el año 2022 sumado a la gran cobertura del programa de inmunización para Covid-19 e influenza con un gran despliegue de los equipos en el territorio .

column20: Health Outcomes Heat-Related Illnesses: Increased Temperatures: Rising temperatures and more frequent heatwaves lead to higher instances of heat-related illnesses, such as heatstroke, dehydration, and heat exhaustion. Vulnerable Populations: The elderly, young children, and individuals with pre-existing health conditions are particularly at risk. Respiratory Issues: Air Quality: Higher temperatures can exacerbate air pollution, increasing the concentration of ground-level ozone and particulate matter. Respiratory Conditions: This deterioration in air quality can lead to a rise in respiratory problems, such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Vector-Borne Diseases: Changing Habitats: Warmer temperatures and altered precipitation patterns can expand the habitats of vectors like mosquitoes and ticks. Disease Spread: This can lead to increased incidence of vector-borne diseases, such as West Nile virus, malaria, and Lyme disease. Waterborne Diseases: Water Quality: Increased temperatures and extreme weather events can degrade water quality, leading to higher risks of waterborne diseases like gastroenteritis. Flooding: Flooding can overwhelm sewage systems, further contaminating water supplies. Mental Health: Stress and Anxiety: The stress and anxiety associated with extreme weather events, displacement, and economic instability can negatively impact mental health. Long-Term Effects: Chronic stress from ongoing climate-related challenges can lead to long-term mental health issues, such as depression and PTSD. Health Services Increased Demand for Healthcare: Heat-Related Emergencies: Higher incidence of heat-related illnesses leads to increased demand for emergency services and hospital admissions. Chronic Conditions: Worsening of chronic respiratory and cardiovascular conditions increases the burden on healthcare facilities. Strain on Healthcare Infrastructure: Resource Allocation: Extreme weather events can disrupt the supply of medical resources, leading to shortages. Facility Damage: Infrastructure damage from storms, flooding, or heatwaves can impair the functionality of healthcare facilities. Public Health Challenges: Disease Surveillance: Increased need for monitoring and controlling the spread of vector- and waterborne diseases. Preventive Measures: Implementation of public health measures to mitigate the impacts of climate change, such as vaccination campaigns and health education. Economic Impacts: Increased Costs: The rising demand for healthcare services and the need for infrastructure resilience can lead to higher healthcare costs. Funding Needs: More funding is required to adapt health services to the growing impacts of climate change, including building climate-resilient healthcare facilities. Emergency Preparedness: Response Plans: Developing and implementing effective emergency response plans for extreme weather events. Training: Training healthcare professionals to manage the health impacts of climate change effectively. Adaptation Strategies Enhancing Infrastructure Resilience: Facility Upgrades: Strengthening healthcare infrastructure to withstand extreme weather events. Energy Efficiency: Implementing energy-efficient cooling systems to manage heatwaves. Improving Public Health Systems: Surveillance and Monitoring: Enhancing disease surveillance systems to quickly identify and respond to outbreaks. Public Education: Increasing public awareness about the health risks associated with climate change and preventive measures. Strengthening Healthcare Capacity: Resource Allocation: Ensuring adequate supply of medical resources during extreme weather events. Training Programs: Providing training for healthcare workers on the health impacts of climate change and emergency response.

These demographics heighten the vulnerability of the local health system to climate-related pressures. Rising temperatures and more frequent heatwaves in the Square Mile are expected to place significant strain on health services, which already experience surges in demand during hot weather. This includes increased pressure on emergency response, hospital admissions, and community care services.

The existing built environment further compounds these risks. A substantial portion of the building stock is poorly equipped to manage overheating—56% of domestic EPC ratings issued between 2017-2018 were rated C or lower, and the area includes over 600 listed buildings, many of which are aging and thermally inefficient. Climate change also increases the risk of infectious disease outbreaks, particularly those linked to waterborne and vector-borne pathogens. Warmer temperatures and changing precipitation patterns can expand the habitats of disease-carrying organisms such as mosquitoes, while flooding and overwhelmed drainage systems can lead to contamination of water supplies and increased transmission of gastrointestinal illnesses. These developments would require enhanced surveillance, diagnostics, and response capacity within health systems.
Urban flooding, increasingly likely due to more intense rainfall events, poses further challenges. Flooding can disrupt access to healthcare facilities, damage medical infrastructure, and lead to displacement of vulnerable populations. It also increases the risk of injury, mental health impacts, and exposure to environmental hazards, all of which contribute to higher demand for health services and emergency care.

Additionally, cascading risks such as drought and water supply disruptions during heatwaves, and dehydration-related complications, are likely to intensify demand on health services -—especially for those with chronic conditions. Cold weather also poses challenges, increasing heating demand and associated emissions, further impacting air quality and respiratory health. Overall, climate-related stressors are expected to significantly challenge the resilience and capacity of health systems in the Square Mile.

The climate hazards identified contribute to disruptions in the delivery of health services, as these hazards may overwhelm the health system, particularly when affecting large-scale areas. With limited resources in healthcare and numerous health programs to implement, this issue will inevitably arise if climate hazards are not mitigated or resolved promptly.

Butuan City applies an integrated methodology to understand and address the health effects of climate change-related hazards identified.

The approach begins with data collection and hazard profiling, where City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Department, and partner agencies compile information on rainfall, temperature, flooding extents, coastal surge, and landslide susceptibility. These environmental datasets are complemented by health data from the Field Health Service Information System (FHSIS) of the City Health Department, hospital records, and outbreak surveillance reports, which cover diseases such as diarrhea, leptospirosis, dengue, and respiratory infections. Socio-economic and demographic information, including population distribution, vulnerable groups, and facility locations, are also gathered to establish exposure and sensitivity.

The next step involves hazard characterization and spatial mapping. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are used to overlay hazard maps with health outcomes and population data at the barangay level. This process identifies the geographic overlap between hazard-prone areas and vulnerable populations, highlighting communities at greatest risk.

To capture the interaction between climate hazards and health outcomes, event-based analyses are conducted. For example, disease incidence is recorded, reported, and investigated during a disaster to determine excess cases attributable to it. These statistical techniques help quantify the strength of the relationship between hazards and health outcomes.

A vulnerability and risk assessment framework is then applied, considering three components: hazard intensity, population exposure, and community adaptive capacity. Indicators such as age distribution, water and sanitation access, poverty levels, and health facility readiness are combined into a vulnerability index. This enables the ranking of barangays and facilities based on their overall climate-health risk.

The results are synthesized and used for planning and policy making, which includes maps, priority indicators, and early warning triggers linked to health response measures. The methodology also integrates monitoring and evaluation mechanisms, with regular updates of health and hazard data, to track trends and measure the effectiveness of adaptation interventions.

Key Impacts on Health Outcomes
1. Heat-Related Illnesses 
Quảng Bình frequently experiences extreme heat events and prolonged hot spells, which are intensifying due to climate change.
•	Morbidity: Rising temperatures lead to an increase in heat-related illnesses such as heat exhaustion, heatstroke, and dehydration, resulting in a surge in hospitalizations.
•	Vulnerable Groups: Outdoor workers (like farmers and fishermen), the elderly, young children, and people with pre-existing conditions are particularly at risk.
•	Economic Loss: Heat stress significantly reduces labor productivity, especially for agricultural workers, leading to lost income and economic pressure that can indirectly impact health.
2. Infectious and Vector-Borne Diseases 
Changes in temperature and rainfall patterns create more favorable conditions for disease vectors and pathogens.
•	Vector-Borne Diseases: The altered climate is increasing the suitability for the spread of diseases like dengue fever and other vector-borne diseases.
•	Waterborne Diseases: Increased frequency and intensity of floods and storms contaminate water sources, leading to a higher incidence of diarrheal diseases and other waterborne illnesses.
3. Impacts from Extreme Weather Events 
As a coastal province frequently hit by storms, floods, and landslides, Quảng Bình faces severe direct health risks.
•	Injury and Mortality: Severe floods and flash floods, such as the historic events in October 2020, cause direct injuries, drowning, and loss of life.
•	Displacement and Mental Health: Mass displacement and damage to homes and livelihoods lead to significant mental health stress, anxiety, depression, and trauma among affected communities, particularly in poor coastal and mountainous communes.
•	Infrastructure Damage: Flooding damages critical infrastructure, including health facilities and roads, disrupting access to essential healthcare services precisely when they are most needed.
4. Food and Water Security
Climate impacts threaten the basic determinants of health, especially in vulnerable, low-income communities.
•	Saline Intrusion and Drought: Increased saltwater intrusion and drought conditions negatively affect agricultural output and fishing, threatening food security and nutrition.
•	Water Quality: Reduced water availability during droughts and contaminated sources after floods compromise the supply of clean drinking water, escalating health risks.

Climate change severely impacts the health system's capacity and resilience in Quảng Bình Province by simultaneously increasing the burden of disease and physically disrupting service delivery, particularly during and after extreme weather events.
1. Increased Service Demand and Strain 
Climate change multiplies health risks, directly overloading the local healthcare system:
•	Surge in Climate-Sensitive Diseases: The system experiences sudden spikes in patient load due to:
o	Heat-Related Illnesses: During prolonged, intense heatwaves.
o	Infectious Disease Outbreaks: After floods, which increase the spread of waterborne illnesses (diarrhea, cholera) and vector-borne diseases (dengue fever) due to contaminated water and stagnant pools.
•	Mental Health Burden: Increased demand for psychological and mental health support following major disasters (storms, severe floods) that cause loss of life, property, and livelihood.
•	Chronic Strain: The long-term effects of climate change, such as malnutrition from agricultural losses, worsen chronic conditions, adding to the daily workload of communal health stations and provincial hospitals.
2. Infrastructure Damage and Access Disruption 
Extreme weather events directly compromise the physical ability of the health system to function:
•	Physical Damage to Facilities: Storms and severe floods can damage or inundate health facilities, especially local-level Commune Health Stations (CHSs) in low-lying or rural areas, rendering them inoperable or destroying essential equipment and medicine stocks.
•	Interruption of Access: Flooding and landslides cut off road access to hospitals and clinics. This prevents patients from reaching care and stops health workers from reporting to duty or delivering crucial supplies (vaccines, medications) to isolated areas.
•	Power and Water Loss: Disasters frequently lead to power outages and contamination of water supply at health facilities, making it impossible to perform surgeries, sterilize equipment, or maintain sanitation, severely degrading the quality of care.
3. Supply Chain and Resource Scarcity 
Climate-related disruptions affect the operational backbone of the health system:
•	Drug and Equipment Shortages: Flooding can destroy or spoil medical supplies in storage at local health posts. Furthermore, transport disruption due to damaged roads and bridges delays the delivery of essential drugs, vaccines, and clean water supplies from central warehouses.
•	Financial Strain: The health system incurs higher emergency costs for disaster response (e.g., mobile medical teams, post-flood sanitation, procurement of emergency supplies) while simultaneously facing revenue loss from non-functioning facilities and damaged infrastructure repairs.
•	Workforce Challenges: Health workers in disaster-prone areas face burnout, physical danger, and personal losses, which compromise their ability and willingness to maintain service delivery during and immediately after a crisis.

System Vulnerability and Adaptation
The health system in Quảng Bình, like much of Central Vietnam, has a high level of exposure to climate hazards, and while the Vietnamese government has national plans to improve health sector adaptation, the local adaptive capacity is often constrained by limited resources, especially at the grassroots level.

Key adaptation priorities for the system include:

Climate-Proofing Infrastructure: Building or retrofitting health facilities in flood-prone areas (e.g., using raised foundations, resilient building materials).

Early Warning and Surveillance: Integrating climate-informed surveillance systems to better predict and prepare for outbreaks of climate-sensitive diseases (like dengue and diarrheal illness).

Capacity Building: Training health workers in disaster emergency response, first aid, and mental health support in post-disaster settings.

Impactos del cambio climático en la salud y los servicios de salud en el municipio Maneiro

El sistema de salud en el municipio Manuel Plácido Maneiro, dentro del estado Nueva Esparta, enfrenta limitaciones estructurales y operativas que reducen su capacidad de respuesta ante los impactos del cambio climático. Estas debilidades, combinadas con la insularidad del territorio, agravan los riesgos sobre la salud de la población y comprometen la resiliencia comunitaria.

1. Infecciones y enfermedades transmitidas por el agua
La variabilidad climática y los eventos extremos generan interrupciones en el acceso a agua segura, aumentando la incidencia de enfermedades gastrointestinales y otras patologías transmitidas por agua contaminada. Esto se ve agravado por la limitada capacidad de tratamiento y saneamiento en el municipio.

2. Interrupción en la provisión de servicios de agua, saneamiento y aguas residuales, y en la accesibilidad a los servicios
Los cortes prolongados de agua y la irregularidad en el suministro dificultan la higiene personal y comunitaria, incrementando los riesgos sanitarios. La falta de continuidad en estos servicios también impacta directamente la capacidad operativa de ambulatorios y hospitales.

3. Interrupción de los servicios relacionados con la salud
Las deficiencias en el suministro eléctrico e hídrico afectan la operatividad de los centros de salud, limitando la atención de emergencias durante olas de calor, inundaciones o brotes epidémicos.

4. Infecciones y enfermedades transmitidas por los alimentos
El incremento de las temperaturas acelera la descomposición de los alimentos y aumenta los riesgos de intoxicaciones, particularmente en un municipio con alta dependencia del turismo y el consumo de productos pesqueros.

5. Enfermedades relacionadas con el calor
El aumento de olas de calor provoca golpes de calor, deshidratación y agotamiento físico. Adultos mayores, niños y personas con enfermedades crónicas constituyen los grupos más vulnerables.

6. Exacerbación de los síntomas de enfermedades no transmisibles: cardiovasculares y respiratorias
Las temperaturas extremas y la mala calidad del aire agravan enfermedades cardiovasculares y respiratorias, como hipertensión, asma o EPOC, incrementando hospitalizaciones y mortalidad en la población afectada.

7. Impactos en la salud espiritual y/o emocional
El estrés por condiciones ambientales extremas y la exposición recurrente a crisis sanitarias y de servicios básicos generan ansiedad, depresión y otros problemas de salud mental. Esto afecta la cohesión comunitaria y la capacidad de respuesta ante emergencias.

8. Infecciones y enfermedades transmitidas por vectores
El aumento de la temperatura y los cambios en los patrones de precipitación favorecen la proliferación de mosquitos transmisores de dengue, zika y chikungunya. Esto representa un riesgo significativo en zonas residenciales con problemas de drenaje y agua estancada.

9. Daños y destrucción de la tecnología e infraestructura de salud, incluidos los modos de acceso
Eventos climáticos extremos como lluvias intensas o inundaciones afectan la infraestructura de salud, dificultando la atención de emergencias. El acceso a los centros de salud también se ve comprometido cuando las vías quedan intransitables por acumulación de agua o desechos.

10. Lesiones físicas directas o fallecimientos debido a condiciones climáticas extremas
Aunque menos frecuentes, las tormentas, marejadas y otros fenómenos costeros pueden generar muertes o traumatismos, especialmente en poblaciones asentadas cerca de la costa o en viviendas precarias.
